name: Ampullary tumours
lead: Which gate this patient is at, and the one error this disease punishes hardest: treating a biopsy that reads adenoma as though it had excluded the carcinoma underneath it.
gatelabel: The decision in front of you

gates.name: 0 · Presentation, workup and local extent
crit: Pancreatic-protocol CT of the abdomen and pelvis plus CT chest, before elective instrumentation
Duodenoscopy with a side-viewing instrument, with targeted biopsies, and colonoscopy if not already done
EUS and MRI with MRCP where an endoscopic resection is being considered or intraductal extension is in question
Liver function tests, baseline CA 19-9 and CEA
The epicentre recorded — ampulla, non-ampullary duodenum or distal bile duct — because that is what sets the prognosis
gates.ask: Do I know where this tumour actually starts, how deep it goes and how far up the ducts it runs — and did I get that before anyone put a stent across it?

standard.t: Look at the papilla with a side-viewing duodenoscope, not a forward-viewing gastroscope, and describe the lesion by compartment: ampullary-duodenal, intra-ampullary, or ampullary-ductal.
standard.pref: Every suspected ampullary neoplasm. NCCN specifies a side-viewing endoscope in the workup. PERIPAN asks endoscopists to classify the lesion as ampullary-duodenal (visible change on the duodenal surface) or as sitting inside the ampulla, and to say when it looks like an intra-ampullary papillary tubular neoplasm — an elevated papilla covered by relatively preserved mucosa — because that tells the pathologist what to cut for.
standard.avoid: Do not accept a forward-viewing look as the examination. In familial adenomatous polyposis a short transparent cap on a gastroscope visualised the duodenum and ampulla in 95% of patients, so cap assistance is a workable substitute; an uncapped forward-viewing pass is not.
standard.note: The compartment predicts the histology, and it inverts the usual intuition: ampullary-duodenal tumours are mostly intestinal subtype, while ampullary-ductal tumours — endoscopically the subtle, dimple-like ulcerations — are mostly pancreatobiliary. The unimpressive lesion is the dangerous one. In Adsay's 249-case series the four anatomic subsets had 3-year survival of 73% (intra-ampullary papillary-tubular-neoplasm-associated, n=61), 69% (periampullary-duodenal, n=12), 41% (ampullary-ductal, n=36) and 54% (ampullary-NOS, n=140, 55% of cases). Read in full the ordering is softer than the numbers suggest: the omnibus log-rank across the four groups at 1 year gave P=0.167, and the authors call the subsets prognostically distinct on pairwise comparison of the Kaplan-Meier curves rather than on a significant overall test. No confidence interval is given for any estimate anywhere in the paper, no multivariable model adjusting for T stage, nodes or invasion size is reported although one is described in the methods, the favourable periampullary-duodenal group has 12 patients of whom 6 were node positive, and invasion size — the variable that drives the ordering — was in part derived by applying an invasive-to-non-invasive ratio read off the slides to the gross size rather than measured. The categories were assigned retrospectively by the same authors who devised the scheme, with no blinded reassignment and no interobserver statistic, so the reproducibility of the gross algorithm the whole classification rests on is untested. Use the compartment to tell the pathologist what to cut for, not to give a prognosis. [EXPERTISE]

standard.t: Add EUS and MRI with MRCP before committing to an endoscopic resection, and record intraductal extension as a length, not as a yes or no.
standard.pref: Any lesion that might be taken endoscopically. ESGE recommends EUS and abdominal MRCP for staging ampullary tumours (strong recommendation, low quality evidence) and NCCN suggests EUS in all lesions that might be removed endoscopically, to assess intraductal or parenchymal invasion. Against surgical pathology as the reference, EUS in 102 patients gave 80% sensitivity and 93% specificity for any intraductal extension, accuracy 91%, AUROC 0.87 (95% CI 0.76–0.97), and ERCP in 81 patients gave 83% and 93%, accuracy 84%, AUROC 0.88 (0.77–0.99). Overall EUS accuracy for local tissue invasion was 90% (90 of 100).
standard.avoid: Do not treat EUS as a reliable way to separate an adenoma from a T1 cancer, and read the headline accuracy by stage rather than overall. The 90% figure is carried almost entirely by correctly calling 65 of 66 lesions confined to the ampulla: accuracy was 98% for T1 but 78% for T2, 80% for T3 and 78% for T4, with 7 patients understaged (duodenal wall 4, pancreas 1, other structures 2) and 3 overstaged — so EUS systematically understages in exactly the categories that would change the operation. A separate 120-patient series reporting overall T-stage accuracy of 81.7% with 93.9% sensitivity and 45.5% specificity for the adenoma/T1 category, 50.0% sensitivity for T2 and nodal accuracy 75.0% with N1 sensitivity 62.5% is cited here from its abstract only — the full text was not obtained. Either way, a node-negative EUS does not establish N0.
standard.note: Compared against ERCP rather than surgical pathology, EUS sensitivity for intraductal extension fell to 56% with 97% specificity (accuracy 90%, AUROC 0.77, 95% CI 0.64–0.89), missing 6 of 12 bile duct extensions, so the reference standard changes the answer. Three limits that the full text makes clear. First, the reference standard is partly circular for the lesions that matter most: in endoscopically resected adenomas, absence of intraductal extension was assumed whenever resection was complete with a negative margin and cholangiography was clear, which already incorporates endoscopic judgement and inflates specificity and accuracy. Second, the three comparisons use non-overlapping subsets of the same cohort (90, 102 and 81 patients) selected by whether an ERCP or a resection specimen existed, so EUS and ERCP were not read in the same patients and the claim that they perform similarly is not a paired comparison. Third, sensitivity rests on 9 to 12 patients with intraductal extension, which is why the intervals are wide. Two incidental findings from the same series are worth carrying: 10 of 58 papillectomy specimens (17%) proved non-adenomatous despite an outside biopsy reported as adenoma, and EUS-FNA diagnosed adenocarcinoma in 6 of 7 (86%) but adenoma or advanced adenoma in only 1 of 5 (20%).

standard.t: Do not place a biliary stent before planned surgery as a routine; stent for cholangitis or fever, for severe symptomatic jaundice, or when the operation is being delayed, including for neoadjuvant therapy.
standard.pref: This is NCCN's stent position for ampullary adenocarcinoma, and the randomised evidence behind it is strong but borrowed: in 202 patients with cancer of the pancreatic head, preoperative biliary drainage raised serious complications within 120 days from 39% to 74% (relative risk for early surgery 0.54, 95% CI 0.41–0.71, P<0.001). ERCP-guided drainage is preferred over the percutaneous route when drainage is needed, stents should be as short as feasible, and a fully covered self-expanding metal stent is preferred when neoadjuvant therapy is planned because it can be exchanged or removed.
standard.avoid: Read the limits honestly, because they are larger than the headline. That trial enrolled cancer of the pancreatic head — 92% of the 196 patients had adenocarcinoma, site was carried only as a pancreatic-versus-periampullary covariate and no ampullary subgroup result is reported anywhere. Bilirubin was 40–250 µmol/L. Surgery-related complications alone did not differ (early surgery 35 of 94, 37%, versus drainage 48 of 102, 47%; relative risk 0.79, 95% CI 0.57–1.11, P=0.14), so on the question clinicians actually ask — does operating on a jaundiced patient carry more surgical risk — the trial is null. The entire excess was procedural: drainage-related complications occurred in 47 of 102 (46%) against 2 of 94 (2%), dominated by cholangitis in 27 patients (26%), stent occlusion in 15 (15%) and a need for stent exchange in 31 (30%). Mortality did not differ (any cause 12 of 94, 13%, versus 15 of 102, 15%; relative risk 0.85, 0.42–1.72) and median stay was 14 against 16 days. NCCN also states that a self-expanding metal stent should only be placed once a tissue diagnosis is confirmed — an uncovered metal stent in an undiagnosed papilla is a self-inflicted problem.
standard.note: Downgraded from B to C on the full-text read, and the reason is not the trial's conduct but what it tested and in whom. The intervention was a 10 Fr plastic endoprosthesis left for 4 to 6 weeks; the authors' own closing recommendation is that drainage during neoadjuvant treatment might be better achieved with metal stents, which concedes that the intervention tested is not the one now used. The design was a noninferiority comparison with a 10 percentage-point margin and one-sided alpha 0.05, and it is universally cited as showing that drainage causes harm. Only 61% of patients went on to resection and 31% had a palliative bypass, and the palliative subgroup showed the largest difference (surgical complications 18 of 33, 55%, versus 5 of 28, 18%, P=0.003) — so the result is partly driven by patients in whom stenting would now be definitive therapy rather than preparation. Events were counted to 120 days from randomisation, which gives the drainage arm a 4 to 6 week period at risk with no equivalent in the early-surgery arm. Separately, a stent across the papilla degrades the endoscopic and EUS assessment that the papillectomy decision depends on, which is a second and ampullary-specific reason to stage first where the clinical situation allows.

standard.t: Name the tumour by its epicentre and stop writing periampullary once the specimen is in hand — ampullary, duodenal, distal bile duct and pancreatic head cancers share an operation and not a prognosis.
standard.pref: PERIPAN defines ampullary carcinoma as arising from any segment of the ampulla of Vater, distal cholangiocarcinoma as having its epicentre in the common bile duct above the sphincter of Oddi with no or minimal ampullary involvement, and duodenal carcinoma as having its epicentre in the non-ampullary duodenum. It recommends that periampullary be avoided in pathology reports and cancer-registry submissions, and used before resection only when imaging cannot identify the epicentre.
standard.avoid: Do not let the shared Whipple collapse the distinction. Pancreatobiliary-predominant ampullary carcinoma — the worst-prognosis tubular ampullary group — still had median survival of 41 months against 15.6 months for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, and 1.97 times the hazard of death (95% CI 1.42–2.72, P<0.001) when matched for size and node status; in Adsay's series the ampullary-ductal subset's 3-year survival was 41% against 11% for 113 pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas. The distinction does not change the operation; it changes what you tell the patient and how you read every adjuvant study.
standard.note: PERIPAN is explicit that the historical habit of pooling these tumours is why the adjuvant literature cannot be reconciled: inconsistent definitions and high interobserver variability have hindered consistent conclusions, particularly about adjuvant chemotherapy. There is a corollary that cuts the other way and belongs here. Applying the strict epicentre definition reclassified 68 of 317 previously labelled ampullary cases (21%) as pancreatic (33), duodenal (16) or common bile duct (19) carcinomas secondarily involving the ampulla. Removing those cases removes mostly the worst-prognosis tumours, so part of the survival gap between ampullary carcinoma and pancreatic cancer in the modern literature is a definitional effect rather than a biological one. The comparator cohorts in that series were convenience groups from the same archives with no matching for stage, size or treatment, and adjuvant therapy was not recorded at all.

alt.t: ERCP or percutaneous cholangiography when cross-sectional imaging and EUS leave the ductal extent unresolved — accepting the added morbidity.
alt.pref: An indeterminate stricture, or a lesion where the length of intraductal growth will decide between papillectomy and resection. ERCP matched surgical pathology as well as EUS did for intraductal extension (83% sensitivity, 93% specificity).
alt.avoid: NCCN notes that ERCP and PTC add diagnostic capability beyond EGD, EUS and CT but carry increased morbidity and even mortality. Do not order one to confirm what EUS and MRCP have already established.
alt.note: Intraductal ultrasound at the same session performed well in the one series reporting it — sensitivity 87.5%, specificity 92.5% and accuracy 90.2% for carcinoma in 72 patients, with T-stage accuracy 86%, 71% and 86% for T1, T2 and T3 and nodal accuracy 75% — but that paper is cited here from its abstract only; the full text was not obtained, so its selection, blinding and reference standard cannot be checked. ESGE itself only suggests intraductal ultrasound in selected patients, with routine use balanced against training, cost and pancreatitis risk. Note too that the EUS-against-ERCP comparison behind this string is not a paired one: the two tests were compared in different, availability-selected subsets of the same cohort. [EXPERTISE]

alt.t: PET/CT when MRI cannot be performed, and MRI for indeterminate liver lesions.
alt.pref: NCCN's own sequence: MRI for indeterminate liver lesions as clinically indicated, with PET/CT substituted when MRI is not possible, such as in a pacemaker-dependent patient.
alt.avoid: Not a staging test in its own right in this disease, and no ampullary-specific performance data support it as one.

alt.t: Germline testing at the point of diagnosis, not after the operation.
alt.pref: NCCN recommends genetic testing for inherited mutations in any patient with confirmed ampullary adenocarcinoma or a positive family history, using comprehensive hereditary-cancer panels, with counselling for anyone positive for ATM, BRCA1, BRCA2, CDKN2A, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PALB2, PMS2, STK11 or TP53, or with a positive family history regardless of mutation status. The supporting ampullary data are much thinner than the recommendation: in a nationwide Dutch series of 90 resected carcinomas diagnosed under age 50, mismatch-repair deficiency was found in 11 of 23 duodenal carcinomas (47.8%) but only 1 of 23 ampullary (4.3%) and 2 of 44 pancreatic (4.5%), and it was that single ampullary patient and those two pancreatic patients in whom deficiency proved attributable to Lynch syndrome.
alt.avoid: Do not quote that series as showing concordance between deficiency and a hereditary cause in ampullary cancer. One of one is not an estimate, no confidence interval appears anywhere in the paper, and the 4.3% ampullary deficiency rate is indistinguishable from pancreatic cancer and lower than the roughly 10% to 15% reported in unselected ampullary series — which would mean selecting by young age performs worse than testing everyone, the opposite of the paper's framing. The cohort is also resection-specimens-only from 23 cooperating laboratories, with 72 of 162 eligible patients (44%) not included because material was not supplied and no comparison of included against excluded patients offered. The case for germline testing at diagnosis rests on NCCN's recommendation and on the family consequences of a positive result, not on this prevalence estimate.

avoid.t: Do not stage this tumour on a portal-venous CT of the abdomen alone.
avoid.pref: Use the pancreatic protocol with chest imaging, and add EUS and MRCP when an endoscopic resection is in question.
avoid.avoid: A single-phase abdominal CT answers neither the depth question nor the intraductal-extension question, and both decide the operation.

avoid.t: Do not let a self-expanding metal stent be placed across an undiagnosed papilla.
avoid.pref: NCCN: metal stents only once tissue diagnosis is confirmed; a removable or fully covered stent where the diagnosis or the plan is still open.
avoid.avoid: It forecloses endoscopic resection, distorts the specimen, and in a patient who turns out to have a benign adenoma it was never needed.

gates.name: 1 · The biopsy says adenoma — what is underneath it
crit: High-grade dysplasia anywhere in the biopsy
Bile duct or pancreatic duct dilatation on imaging
Symptoms — jaundice, pancreatitis, weight loss, pain
Age 65 or over
Villous architecture, an ulcerated or firm papilla, or a markedly raised CA 19-9 or CEA
gates.ask: How likely is it that there is an invasive carcinoma under this adenoma, and am I about to choose an operation that cannot treat it?

standard.t: Treat a biopsy that reads adenoma as a floor, not a ceiling — the reported false-negative rate for invasive carcinoma beneath an ampullary adenoma is 20% to 40%, and the cause is sampling, not interpretation.
standard.pref: Every patient in whom the management plan rests on the biopsy. NCCN states that endoscopic biopsies of ampullary adenocarcinoma have poor diagnostic accuracy with high false-negative rates of about 20% to 40%, and that final pathology has repeatedly reported carcinoma in lesions initially called adenoma. PERIPAN puts the false-negative rate at 20% to 30% for exactly this distinction and attributes it to sampling bias — the carcinoma within the adenoma not being represented.
standard.avoid: Do not reason from the biopsy to the operation as if the two were the same question. In a 10-year single-institution series, 90 of 252 patients with an ampullary biopsy had a follow-up biopsy or resection specimen; 55 (61.1%) were concordant and 35 (38.9%) discordant, with 8 of the 35 discordances (22.9%, and 8.9% of the 90) a major one — and all 8 were a benign biopsy with a malignant resection, 7 of them attributed to superficial sampling and only 1 to interpretive error. In 44 endoscopic papillectomies done for lesions judged benign, 14 (32%) harboured adenocarcinoma missed on the prior biopsies: invasive adenocarcinoma in 9 (20.5%) and adenoma with intramucosal carcinoma in a further 5 (11.3%), with a further 5 (11.3%) non-adenomatous lesions wrongly called adenoma.
standard.note: This is the single most consequential error in this disease, and it is not reducible by more biopsies alone. PERIPAN: acquisition of biopsy material from the accurate site is key and more important than the number of biopsies — but it recommends a minimum of three targeted biopsies of viable abnormal tissue, because fewer than three is a sampling choice masquerading as a result. Both supporting series understate the problem rather than overstate it, and in opposite ways. The 8.9% major-discrepancy rate is computed on the 36% of patients who had follow-up pathology, and those are precisely the patients whose biopsy or clinical picture raised concern, so it is a lower bound. The 32% occult-carcinoma rate comes from a cohort in which 35 of the original 79 papillectomies (44.3%) had already been excluded for a malignant biopsy or a suspicious endoscopic appearance — it is the rate after the obviously malignant lesions were removed. The same institutional series reports biopsy sensitivity for malignancy of 60% (12 of 20) and cytology 56% (5 of 9), rising to 89% (8 of 9) combined, but those are 9-to-20-patient estimates with no confidence intervals, cytology was ordered in 88% of non-ampullary periampullary but only 17% of ampullary tumours, and 3 of 5 pathologists knew the malignant cytology result before signing out the biopsy — so the incremental value of adding cytology is not estimable from these data.

standard.t: Score the malignancy risk explicitly before choosing between an endoscopic and an open operation, rather than carrying an unstated impression into the decision.
standard.pref: Any biopsy-proven adenoma where the choice of operation is live. In 127 non-familial periampullary adenomas taken to pancreatoduodenectomy at 8 institutions, 59 (46.4%) proved malignant on final pathology; age 65 or over (odds ratio 3.2, 95% CI 1.3–7.9), bile duct 9 mm or more (3.3, 1.4–10.1), any preoperative symptom (7.7, 2.1–26.8) and high-grade dysplasia on biopsy (7.5, 2.6–19.8) were independent predictors, weighted into a 0–6 score (age 1, duct 1, symptoms 2, high-grade dysplasia 2). In a separate 91-patient cohort, cited here from its abstract only because the full text was not obtained, the malignancy rate after resection of a biopsy-proven adenoma was 26.4%, with high-grade dysplasia (odds ratio 6.86, 95% CI 1.58–29.79) and ductal dilatation (11.12, 2.27–54.37) independent predictors.
standard.avoid: Do not use the score to justify a Whipple in the low-risk group: in that series the patients at no or low risk had a higher rate of major postoperative complications than the intermediate and high-risk groups, though the three-group comparison was not significant (51.7%, 27.1% and 29.4%, P=0.11) and significance appeared only after the strata were collapsed at a score of 3 and adjusted for comorbidity, obesity, duct size and parenchymal texture (odds ratio 2.9, 95% CI 1.01–8.6, P=0.047). The simpler reading of that inversion is physiological rather than prognostic: patients with benign pathology have soft, non-atrophic glands and non-dilated ducts because nothing is obstructing them, and fistula risk follows gland texture and duct size. The score is a shared-decision instrument, and the authors present it as one.
standard.note: Downgraded from C to D on the full-text read, and the recommendation to score explicitly stands while the score itself should not be quoted to a patient as a calibrated risk. Four reasons. The score was derived and evaluated in the same 127 patients with no split sample, no bootstrap, no c-statistic, no calibration plot and no sensitivity or specificity at any threshold, and the authors state that validation was impossible. Its strata appear three different ways in the same paper: the abstract gives low risk n=26, intermediate 59 and high 26 with malignancy rates of 10.3%, 44.1% and 88.2%, the results text gives 11.5%, 41.7% and 84.6%, and Table 4 gives 3 of 29, 26 of 59 and 30 of 34 — so the calibration cannot be checked from the published data. Every patient in the cohort had a pancreatoduodenectomy, so the score is calibrated on a population already judged to need resection, which is not the population facing the choice. And two of its four components — any preoperative symptom, worth 2 points on a list that includes fatigue, nausea and dark urine, and a bile duct of 9 mm or more — are proxies for obstruction rather than for neoplastic progression; jaundice and biliary stenting were dropped from the model as redundant with symptoms, which concedes the point. Lesion size did not predict malignancy (median 2.9 against 3.5 cm, P=0.3, missing in 27 of 127) and EUS findings are absent from the paper entirely. [REGISTRY]

standard.t: For a deep or intra-ampullary lesion that forceps cannot reach, use EUS-guided fine-needle biopsy rather than aspiration or brushings.
standard.pref: Hard-to-reach, deep-seated intra-ampullary lesions — typically ampullary-ductal carcinoma or an intra-ampullary papillary tubular neoplasm covered by intact or ulcerated mucosa. PERIPAN recommends EUS-FNB here, and prefers core biopsy over cytology because the distinction between reactive and neoplastic atypia on cytology is extremely challenging and because tissue permits immunohistochemistry and molecular work.
standard.avoid: Do not rely on aspiration or brushings alone. In one 72-patient series transpapillary forceps biopsy by itself detected 68.7% of carcinomas — a false-negative rate of 31.3% — with 100% specificity, and combining it with intraductal ultrasound raised sensitivity to 97% and accuracy to 94.5%; that paper is cited from its abstract only, since the full text was not obtained, so treat the increment as a direction rather than a number. The general point does not depend on it: in a separate series EUS-FNA diagnosed adenocarcinoma in 6 of 7 cases but adenoma or advanced adenoma in only 1 of 5.
standard.note: EUS-FNA or brushings may be added to FNB to raise yield in difficult cases, but not substituted for it.

alt.t: Resample, once, with the endoscopic compartment named on the request form — then stop.
alt.pref: A non-diagnostic or discordant first biopsy where the compartment was not stated. PERIPAN is explicit that precise information on the site of the lesion relative to the duodenum, ampullary channel, bile duct, pancreatic duct and pancreas, and the presence or absence of intracanalicular growth, changes how the specimen is cut: if ampullary-ductal origin is suspected from the dimple-like endoscopic appearance, the pathologist takes deeper sections to look for subtle cancer growth.
alt.avoid: Do not keep resampling in pursuit of a negative result that will not change the plan. If a third negative biopsy would not alter the operation, the patient needs a decision, not another endoscopy — and each ampullary biopsy carries a pancreatitis risk.
alt.note: In a prospective screening series of 102 patients with familial polyposis the papilla was abnormal in 87 of 97 biopsied there, and among the 80 patients biopsied at both sites the papilla was twice as likely to be adenomatous as the peripapillary area (81% against 41%) — so an ampullary biopsy in polyposis is high-yield and is also why it is now discouraged. The harm figure most often quoted, that 30% of available tests showed an asymptomatic amylase rise after ampullary biopsy in a prospective series of 35 polyposis patients, together with a handful of case reports of acute pancreatitis, reaches this page through a narrative review rather than from the primary studies; that review has no protocol, no second reviewer, no risk-of-bias appraisal and no pooling, so the figure is an unweighted quotation. If a biopsy of the ampulla is unavoidable, taking it from the 9-to-1-o'clock sector, away from the pancreatic orifice, has been suggested.

alt.t: Report high-risk features and tumour budding on the biopsy, even when T and N stage cannot be assessed.
alt.pref: Any biopsy or ampullectomy specimen. PERIPAN asks for presence of non-invasive neoplasia versus invasive carcinoma, histological type including poorly cohesive morphology, grade, lymphatic, vascular and perineural invasion, and tumour budding. High budding — three or more budding foci per ×200 field — is reported as an independent predictor of overall survival with a stronger prognostic impact than tumour stage or nodal metastasis.
alt.avoid: Do not over-read a budding score from a biopsy. PERIPAN acknowledges that the invasive front, where budding should be assessed, may not be represented in the biopsy at all. Note also what the claim rests on: the threshold of three or more budding foci per ×200 field has no reproducibility data of its own, the prognostic claim comes largely from the same institutional tradition that produced the ampullary subtype classification, and PERIPAN grades the recommendation low evidence and weak. Budding is reported because it may be the only prognostic variable available in a specimen that cannot be staged, not because it has been validated against T and N stage in independent cohorts.

avoid.t: Do not perform a papillectomy to obtain a diagnosis when adenoma has not been proven.
avoid.pref: Prove the adenoma first. This is ESGE's first recommendation in ampullary tumours and it is a strong recommendation on low-quality evidence.
avoid.avoid: The cost of ignoring it is measurable, and it is the most important single finding in the European comparison of these two operations. Final histology was neither adenoma nor adenocarcinoma — mostly hyperplastic or chronic inflammatory tissue — in 270 of 1,115 endoscopic papillectomy patients (24.2%) and 25 of 169 transduodenal surgical ampullectomy patients (14.8%), while advanced cancer (T2 or above, or node positive) was found in 122 papillectomy (10.9%) and 62 surgical ampullectomy (36.6%) patients. Roughly a third of the procedures in each arm were therefore performed for the wrong indication: either there was no neoplasm to remove, or the disease was already beyond what a local resection can treat. The authors call the rate of poor indications still high for both operations.

avoid.t: Do not subtype the carcinoma on the biopsy in order to drive definitive treatment when the patient is going to resection.
avoid.pref: PERIPAN: subtyping and biomarker assessment on biopsy material should be done only if it may influence subsequent treatment — that is, mainly in a patient who may not have surgery. Otherwise subtype and test for mismatch-repair deficiency on the resection specimen.
avoid.avoid: About 40% of ampullary carcinomas show a mixed or hybrid phenotype — 94 of 232 cases by consensus of three of five blinded observers, against pure pancreatobiliary in 74 (32%) and pure intestinal in only 13 (6%) — so the subtype seen in a biopsy may not represent the tumour. The reproducibility study that established this warns explicitly that caution is warranted when applying the classification to biopsies and tissue microarrays, and in its own side experiment two fields from a single tumour shown blind to eight observers were called pancreatobiliary by 6 of 8 and hybrid by 2 of 8 for one field, and intestinal by 4 of 8 and mixed by 4 of 8 for the other. It also selected tumours with an invasive component over 3.0 mm, which removes the small intra-ampullary lesions that a biopsy is most likely to represent.

gates.name: 2 · Endoscopic papillectomy
crit: Adenoma proven on biopsy, with no suspicion of invasive carcinoma — high-grade dysplasia alone does not exclude the operation
No intraductal extension, or extension short enough that the resection can clear it
Size that can be taken en bloc — ESGE sets 20 to 30 mm as the ceiling for an en bloc intent
Duodenal anatomy that permits access, with no diverticulum preventing it
A high-volume centre, and a patient who will attend surveillance for at least five years
gates.ask: Can I take this out in one piece with a clear deep margin, and will this patient still be coming back to me in five years?

standard.t: Endoscopic papillectomy by direct snare resection without submucosal injection, aiming at en bloc removal, at a high-volume centre.
standard.pref: Ampullary adenoma without intraductal extension. ESGE recommends papillectomy in this group (strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence), recommends en bloc resection of adenomas up to 20–30 mm to achieve R0 and reduce recurrence (strong, low quality), and recommends direct snare resection without submucosal injection (strong, moderate quality). NCCN agrees that adenomas without suspicion of adenocarcinoma, including those with high-grade dysplasia, may be safely removed endoscopically, and that this should be done at a high-volume centre.
standard.avoid: Do not take on a lesion that cannot be reached or encircled, and do not improvise an en bloc attempt above 30 mm. ESGE suggests surgery when endoscopic resection is not feasible for technical reasons such as a diverticulum or size over 4 cm, and when intraductal involvement exceeds 20 mm — with surveillance still mandatory afterwards.
standard.note: Submucosal injection is specifically not recommended: it lifts the mucosa away from the ductal structures the snare needs to engage and makes the anatomy harder, not easier. ESGE grades that recommendation strong on moderate-quality evidence, which the subsequent literature does not quite support — the 2025 European comparison of papillectomy with surgical ampullectomy notes that the evidence remains contradictory and that submucosal injection was still used in 24.2% of its matched endoscopic cases. The more useful warning about en bloc intent is that technical success and histological completeness are different things: in 798 Japanese patients, en bloc resection was achieved in 89.0% and technical success in 94.9%, yet only 58.6% of en bloc resections (416 of 710) were ultimately R0, the rest downgraded by thermal artefact or margin involvement. An en bloc resection is a better starting point for a margin assessment, not a guarantee of one. [EXPERTISE]

standard.t: Place a prophylactic pancreatic duct stent, and use a wire-guided technique if that is what it takes to get the stent in.
standard.pref: Every papillectomy. ESGE recommends prophylactic pancreatic duct stenting to reduce post-papillectomy pancreatitis (strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence). In the only randomised trial of the stent itself, 19 patients were allocated after en bloc snare ampullectomy; pancreatitis within 24 hours occurred in 3 of 9 analysed unstented patients (33%) and none of 10 stented patients (P=0.02). In practice the stent is placed in the large majority of cases — 93.6% of 798 Japanese papillectomies and 73.6% of one 106-patient Korean cohort, where stenting was associated with less pancreatitis on multivariable analysis (odds ratio 0.205, 95% CI 0.044–0.945, P=0.042).
standard.avoid: Give both halves when consenting, because the randomised evidence is weaker than the recommendation it supports. That 19-patient trial was stopped early at a pre-specified interim look triggered when the unstented pancreatitis rate reached 30%, against a planned 25 patients per arm, and it reports three different results from the same data: 33% against 0% as treated (P=0.02), 25% against 0% excluding the patient in whom stent placement failed (P=0.05), and 25% against 9% by intention to treat, counting that patient in the stented arm, where significance is lost (P=0.3). The outcome window was 24 hours, so bleeding, perforation, papillary stenosis and recurrence were not captured at all. In a 45-patient randomised pilot of wire-guided against conventional papillectomy, the wire-guided technique placed a stent in 22 of 22 (100%) against 15 of 23 (65%, P=0.004) but its primary endpoint was negative — pancreatitis 4 of 22 (18%) against 3 of 23 (13%), P=0.960, numerically worse in the arm designed to prevent it. The much-quoted finding inside its conventional arm, pancreatitis in 3 of 8 patients who ended without a stent (37.5%) against 0 of 15 with one (P=0.032), is a post-randomisation comparison between patients who differ precisely by whether bleeding and oedema allowed a stent — that is, by procedural difficulty, which is itself a cause of pancreatitis. The stent probably matters; the route to placing it does not; and neither trial establishes the size of the effect.
standard.note: Downgraded from B to C: the two randomised trials behind this string comprise 64 patients and 10 pancreatitis events between them, one was stopped early and negative on its own intention-to-treat analysis, and the other missed its primary endpoint, so ESGE's grading of moderate-quality evidence overstates what exists. The recommendation stands because the direction is consistent and the intervention is cheap and reversible. Pooled complication figures for endoscopic ampullectomy in the polyposis literature are haemorrhage 4%–21%, pancreatitis 4%–30% and perforation 2%–3%, quoted there as unweighted ranges; in individual cohorts adverse events occurred in 259 of 798 (32.5%, severe in 3.9%, with one procedure-related death), 37 of 136 (27.2%), 26 of 106 (24.5%) and 7 of 44 (15.9%), and the series reporting the lowest rates are also the ones that measured enzymes only in symptomatic patients. [EXPERTISE]

standard.t: Tell the patient before the procedure that about one in five will recur, and that recurrence is late as often as early.
standard.pref: Consent for every papillectomy. In 22 Japanese tertiary centres, 776 patients with confirmed ampullary adenoma or adenocarcinoma had cumulative recurrence of 13% (95% CI 11–16) at 1 year, 20% (17–23) at 3 years and 22% (19–26) at 5 years; R0 resection was achieved in only 416 of 798 (52.1%), with R1 in 176 (22.1%) and an indeterminate Rx margin in 206 (25.8%), and even after R0 cumulative recurrence was 4.9% at 1 year, 11% at 3 years and 13% at 5 years. In a 136-patient single-centre cohort where 124 (91.2%) achieved complete eradication, recurrence occurred in 20 (16.1%) at a mean of 3.2 years, range 0.5 to 9.75 years, a rate of 5.8 per 100 person-years (95% CI 3.6–8.8), and 9 of the 20 recurrences (45%) appeared after the first two years of surveillance.
standard.avoid: Do not present papillectomy as a definitive operation with a short follow-up, and do not quote a single recurrence rate as though the series were measuring the same thing. They are not. The Japanese study counted any histologically confirmed neoplastic tissue, with no requirement for a prior negative surveillance endoscopy, and its median time to recurrence was 6 months (3 months after R1) — so a large fraction of its 18.3% is residual disease. The single-centre study required one negative surveillance endoscopy first and allowed multiple treatment sessions inside its definition of complete eradication, which converts early incomplete resection into a non-event and shifts the curve rightwards. The two 20% figures are not comparable, and the honest statement at consent is that about one in five patients will need further endoscopic treatment of the papilla, early or late. Recurrence rate in the single-centre cohort did not differ by baseline pathology — 5.2 per 100 person-years for low-grade dysplasia, 6.9 for high-grade dysplasia and 7.7 for adenocarcinoma, with overlapping intervals.
standard.note: Margin status is the strongest predictor and is reported twice in the Japanese paper: against R0, the abstract and discussion give hazard ratios of 2.95 (95% CI 1.85–4.71) for R1 and 2.30 (1.44–3.68) for Rx, while Table 2 gives 2.95 (1.87–4.66) and 2.38 (1.49–3.81) for the same comparisons — a small discrepancy, but it means two models were in play and neither is identified. Rx behaved almost identically to frank R1 by 5 years (34% each), which suggests an indeterminate margin is largely an undetected positive one. In a 106-patient Korean cohort a positive or uncertain margin predicted early recurrence (odds ratio 4.023, 95% CI 1.088–16.387, P=0.048) and piecemeal resection predicted late recurrence (6.610, 1.760–24.820, P=0.005) and non-curative resection (5.424, 1.582–18.600, P=0.007) — estimates drawn from 11 to 13 events against 5 or 6 covariates, with intervals spanning an order of magnitude, and with the early-versus-late split defined by the timing of a first surveillance endoscopy that was itself left to the endoscopist. Two further cautions on the timing claim. The Japanese cohort found the later treatment era 2015–2020 an independent predictor of recurrence (hazard ratio 1.57, 1.09–2.26, P=0.016) with no mechanism beyond more procedures by less experienced operators, which could equally be more intensive surveillance. And in the single-centre cohort recurrence was more frequent after en bloc than piecemeal resection (19.4% against 7.0%) and after an initially complete than an incomplete resection (16.5% against 6.1%) — the signature of detection bias in how residual disease was classified, reported in that paper without comment. Its mean follow-up of 2.8 years is also shorter than its mean time to recurrence of 3.2 years, and the single recurrence at 9.75 years is what drives the suggestion of ten-year surveillance.

alt.t: Piecemeal resection with ablation of visible residual tissue, accepting a materially higher recurrence rate, where en bloc is not achievable and the alternative is a pancreatoduodenectomy for a benign lesion.
alt.pref: A large or awkward adenoma in a patient for whom the operative alternative carries real risk. Most patients with a non-curative initial resection in the 106-patient cohort were still managed endoscopically — endoscopic success was 93.4% against curative resection in 76.4%.
alt.avoid: Do not call it equivalent. Piecemeal resection was the independent predictor of both late recurrence (odds ratio 6.610, P=0.005) and non-curative resection (5.424, P=0.007) in one cohort and of recurrence overall in the Japanese national cohort (hazard ratio 1.69, 95% CI 1.07–2.65, P=0.023), and it destroys the margin assessment the next decision depends on. Ablation at the index session is not a rescue either: in the European cohort, 69 of 481 adenoma cases (14.4%) had argon plasma coagulation or radiofrequency ablation during the index papillectomy, and if those are counted as probable R2 resections — which is what visible residual tissue means — the primary success rate of papillectomy alone falls from 80.2% to 65.9% (317 of 481). Retreatment then cascades: of 40 adenoma patients given endoscopic retherapy, 17 (42.5%) were still incomplete at the next follow-up and needed a second session, and 12 of the remaining 15 (80%) needed a third. If the patient's malignancy risk is high, piecemeal papillectomy is the wrong operation rather than a smaller one.
alt.note: Piecemeal resection occurred in 16 of 106 (15.1%) in one cohort and 16 of 44 (36.4%) in another, and en bloc intent failed to deliver an assessable R0 margin in 41% of en bloc Japanese cases, so this is a common situation and worth planning for rather than discovering. Both the 80.2% and the 65.9% figures appear in the European paper without a single preferred estimate, and the reclassification of ablated cases as R2 is the authors' retrospective assumption — a reasonable one, and still an assumption.

alt.t: Papillectomy with close surveillance for high-grade dysplasia or an early carcinoma found after the fact, rather than automatic conversion to resection.
alt.pref: A margin-negative specimen in a patient whose operative risk is substantial. In a propensity-matched Korean multicentre cohort of 127 papillectomies whose final pathology showed high-grade dysplasia or adenocarcinoma, drawn from 485 papillectomies in a 1,607-patient registry, 5-year overall survival was 89.2% with papillectomy alone (22 matched patients) against 82.3% with subsequent radical surgery (33 patients), P=0.861, over a median follow-up of 43.3 months; unmatched the figures were 91.9% against 82.3%, P=0.443.
alt.avoid: Read the recurrence curves, not the survival curves, and note that two endpoints missed significance in the same direction. Matched 5-year recurrence-free survival was 66.1% with papillectomy alone against 86.7% with surgery, P=0.052, and in the adenocarcinoma-only subgroup (30 against 25 patients) it was 61.4% against 82.6%, P=0.066, with 5-year overall survival 83.2% against 85.0% (P=0.652). A 20-point absolute difference that misses significance in 55 patients is not equivalence. Margin status is what makes surveillance defensible, and it is not a small effect: within the papillectomy-alone group, patients with both lateral and deep margins positive had significantly worse overall survival than those with negative margins (P=0.007) or a positive lateral margin alone (P=0.015), and recurrence-free survival was worse for any positive margin.
alt.note: Downgraded from C to D on the full-text read. T stage is never reported anywhere in the paper — in a cohort where between a third and three-quarters of patients had adenocarcinoma, the absence of any T1a-versus-T1b distinction removes the single variable on which the clinical question turns, since T1b carries a substantially higher nodal metastasis risk. Nodal status is unknown in the papillectomy-alone arm by definition, so the two arms are compared with different information. Immortal time bias is unaddressed and runs against the paper's own conclusion: patients had to survive and remain fit for up to 3 months to enter the surgery arm, while anyone who did not stayed in the papillectomy-alone arm, and no landmark analysis is performed. Matching discarded 72 of 94 papillectomy-alone patients to find 22 matches for 33 surgical patients, inverting the usual ratio, and the groups still differed on the proportion with adenocarcinoma afterwards (63.6% against 75.8%) with no balance diagnostics reported. Allocation was by the treating physician on exactly the variables used for matching, surveillance intensity was left to each of 9 hospitals, and median follow-up of 43.3 months is used to report 5-year survival. The most robust part of that paper is its diagnostic table, which is worth carrying separately: pre-papillectomy forceps biopsy agreed with the papillectomy specimen in 82.1% (300 of 365) of lesions called low-grade dysplasia, 60.3% (35 of 58) called high-grade dysplasia and 91.4% (32 of 35) called adenocarcinoma; of 365 called low-grade, 44 (12.1%) were upgraded after resection, 33 to high-grade dysplasia and 11 to adenocarcinoma.

avoid.t: Do not perform a papillectomy when intraductal extension exceeds 20 mm, when the lesion is over 4 cm, or when a diverticulum prevents access.
avoid.pref: ESGE's own boundary for referring to surgery, with surveillance continuing afterwards either way.
avoid.avoid: The completeness data support the boundary rather than only the opinion, though they are thin: among 58 patients referred for papillectomy, complete resection was achieved in 53 overall (91%) but in only 4 of 5 (80%) with intraductal extension defined by EUS and 4 of 7 (57%) with it defined by ERCP — five and seven patients respectively, so treat the direction as real and the proportions as illustrative. The larger Japanese cohort makes the same point with more patients: where ductal extension was confirmed pathologically, R0 was achieved in only 28 of 137 (20.4%).

avoid.t: Do not discharge a patient after a papillectomy.
avoid.pref: Enrol every patient in the surveillance schedule at gate 9 before the procedure, and say so at consent.
avoid.avoid: Recurrences occurred out to 9.75 years and nearly half appeared after the first two years in the cohort that looked for them longest, so a two-year follow-up programme is designed to miss them. The caveat that belongs with that figure is that the same cohort required a negative surveillance endoscopy before counting an event, which pushes early residual disease out of the recurrence count and the curve to the right; the ten-year recommendation rests on one patient recurring at 9.75 years. What is not in doubt is that recurrence after a histological R0 is common — 11% at 3 years and 13% at 5 years in 416 R0 patients — so a negative margin is not a discharge criterion.

gates.name: 3 · Reading the papillectomy specimen
crit: Deep or lateral margin positive, or indeterminate
Invasive carcinoma in the specimen that was not expected
Resection was piecemeal, so no margin can be assessed
Lymphovascular or perineural invasion, poor differentiation, or high tumour budding
Specimen orientation was not agreed with the pathologist before it was sent
gates.ask: Does this specimen commit me to a pancreatoduodenectomy, or to a surveillance programme?

opts.name: Negative margins, adenoma only — endoscopic surveillance
opts.when: NCCN: patients with ampullary adenoma and negative margins after endoscopic removal should be endoscopically observed.
opts.pref: A complete en bloc resection with clear deep and lateral margins and no invasive component.
opts.avoid: Not a discharge. All patients who have had endoscopic removal or surgical ampullectomy need endoscopic surveillance — only pancreatoduodenectomy for adenoma removes the need.

opts.name: Positive margins, adenoma only — endoscopic re-excision
opts.when: NCCN: patients with positive margins after endoscopic removal can be re-excised, or have surgical ampullectomy or pancreatoduodenectomy.
opts.pref: Residual adenoma that is visible and reachable, in a patient who will tolerate repeated procedures. Most non-curative endoscopic resections are salvaged endoscopically.
opts.avoid: Do not re-excise repeatedly in a patient whose malignancy risk score was high to begin with, or where the deep margin rather than the lateral margin is the problem.

opts.name: Invasive adenocarcinoma in the specimen — pancreatoduodenectomy
opts.when: NCCN: where adenocarcinoma is found, pancreatoduodenectomy. Patients who undergo adenoma resection by pancreatoduodenectomy need no surveillance.
opts.pref: An unexpected invasive carcinoma, particularly with a positive deep margin, lymphovascular or perineural invasion or poor differentiation. This is gate 5 from here.
opts.avoid: A papillectomy specimen cannot stage the nodes, and nodal involvement is frequent even in early T stages — so a decision to stop after papillectomy for invasive disease is a decision to accept unknown nodal status.

standard.order: This is NCCN's algorithm and the order reflects its wording, not a survival comparison — no trial compares these three paths. The one piece of comparative evidence, propensity-matched and retrospective, found no overall survival difference between papillectomy alone and papillectomy followed by surgery for high-grade dysplasia or early carcinoma (89.2% against 82.3% at 5 years, P=0.861), with recurrence-free survival favouring surgery at P=0.052 and 61.4% against 82.6% at P=0.066 in the adenocarcinoma-only subgroup, and margin status the discriminator. That comparison rests on 55 matched patients, never reports T stage, and does not handle the immortal time the surgical arm had to survive to enter it, so it supports surveillance as a defensible option in a margin-negative specimen rather than as an equivalent one.
standard.flagnote: Ratification item: what does this programme do with an invasive carcinoma found incidentally in a margin-negative papillectomy specimen in a fit patient? NCCN routes it to pancreatoduodenectomy; the Korean propensity-matched data support surveillance in selected margin-negative cases; neither answer is evidence-based and the group needs one position rather than one per endoscopist. Registry: specimen findings, decision taken, recurrence and nodal status at any later resection.

standard.t: Agree the orientation and the margins with the pathologist before the specimen leaves the room, in writing.
standard.pref: Every ampullectomy specimen, endoscopic or surgical. NCCN requires either direct communication between the endoscopist or surgeon and the pathologist, or a clearly documented method on the requisition, marking the deep (radial) margin, the duodenal mucosal margin and any other relevant margin. PERIPAN asks for the size of the invasive carcinoma and the margin status to be reported on ampullectomy specimens, and for the specimen to reach the pathology department fresh and be fixed within about 30 minutes.
standard.avoid: Do not let a non-pathologist open or section the specimen, and do not drop a whole specimen into formalin — PERIPAN says both explicitly. If pathology is unavailable, refrigerate.
standard.note: An indeterminate margin is not a neutral result. In the 798-patient Japanese cohort an indeterminate Rx margin carried a hazard ratio of 2.38 for recurrence against R0 (95% CI 1.49–3.81; reported as 2.30, 1.44–3.68 in that paper's abstract), close to the 2.95 for a frankly positive margin, and by 5 years cumulative recurrence after Rx and after R1 was the same at 34% — so an unreadable margin behaves like a positive one. Rx accounted for 206 of 798 specimens (25.8%), which makes this the commonest ambiguous result in the whole pathway and one on which ESGE offers no recommendation at all. Orientation failures manufacture indeterminate margins. Note too that margin status in that cohort was assessed locally at 22 centres with no central review and no interobserver data, which is an argument for writing the local method down rather than for discounting the finding.

alt.t: Surgical ampullectomy as the intermediate step after a failed endoscopic resection of a benign lesion, at a centre with the expertise — see gate 4.
alt.pref: NCCN places surgical ampullectomy between endoscopic re-excision and pancreatoduodenectomy for positive margins after endoscopic removal, and states that it can be chosen at surgical centres where there is expertise for the technique.
alt.avoid: Positive margins after a surgical ampullectomy route the patient on to pancreatoduodenectomy in the same NCCN algorithm, so this is a step that can be spent rather than a destination.
alt.note: In the European cohort, R0 after transduodenal surgical ampullectomy was 90.5% (57 of 63) against 73.1% (416 of 569) after papillectomy (P=0.001), and for adenoma alone 92.9% (53 of 57) against 80.2% (386 of 481, falling to 65.9% once index-session ablation is counted as a probable R2 resection). Two things qualify the comparison. The surgical arm has 63 patients and 6 cancers, so every surgical subgroup figure rests on single-digit numerators, and the only procedure-related death in the study was in that arm. And advanced cancer was found in 36.6% of the surgical specimens against 10.9% of the endoscopic ones, which says as much about who was selected for surgery as about what surgery achieves. [EXPERTISE]

avoid.t: Do not record a piecemeal resection as R0.
avoid.pref: Call it what it is, and let the surveillance interval and the conversion discussion follow from that.
avoid.avoid: Piecemeal resection independently predicted both late recurrence (odds ratio 6.610, P=0.005) and non-curative resection (5.424, P=0.007), and the margin it leaves cannot be assessed. An R-status assigned to an unassessable margin is the start of an avoidable recurrence.

gates.name: 4 · The benign lesion endoscopy cannot clear — ampullectomy or Whipple
crit: Adenoma not clearable endoscopically — size, diverticulum, intraductal extension over 20 mm, or repeated positive margins
No invasive carcinoma demonstrated, and a malignancy risk score that is not high
Patient fit for a transduodenal operation, at a centre that performs them
An ampullary neuroendocrine tumour — which is a different decision and belongs with resection
Familial adenomatous polyposis with Spigelman stage IV disease unsuitable for endoscopic therapy
gates.ask: Is a transduodenal ampullectomy the right-sized operation here, or am I about to under-treat a cancer I have not found?

opts.name: Transduodenal surgical ampullectomy
opts.when: NCCN lists surgical ampullectomy for an adenoma with positive margins after endoscopic removal and states it can be chosen at surgical centres where there is expertise for the technique; it does not list it for invasive carcinoma.
opts.pref: A demonstrably benign adenoma that endoscopy cannot clear, in a patient in whom a pancreatoduodenectomy is a disproportionate operation. In the largest comparison — 569 papillectomies against 63 transduodenal ampullectomies drawn from a 1,673-patient European database of 58 centres — R0 was 90.5% against 73.1% (P=0.001), and for adenoma alone 92.9% against 80.2% (P=0.01); recurrence after a histological R0 was 2 of 63 (3.2%) against 82 of 512 (16.0%), P=0.01; severe adverse events were 2 of 63 (3.2%) against 11 of 569 (1.9%), P=0.38. In 62 propensity-matched pairs, R0 was 90.3% against 72.6% (P=0.02), recurrence 3.2% against 8.0% (P=0.07), reinterventions were more frequent after papillectomy, and overall survival was comparable. The burden difference is the one unambiguous finding: median procedure time 227.5 against 30 minutes and median hospital stay 14 against 3 days (both P<0.001).
opts.avoid: Not for invasive carcinoma, and not for an ampullary neuroendocrine tumour. Downgraded to grade D because the comparison that favours this operation is built in a way that favours it. The 62 matched pairs are 98.4% of the eligible surgical patients but only 10.9% of the eligible papillectomy patients, so the surgical arm is its whole population while the endoscopic arm is a 1-in-9 selection chosen to resemble it. Matching omitted intraductal extension, duct dilation and index-session ablation — the variables that most obviously drive both the choice of procedure and the chance of R0 — and intrabiliary extension and duct dilation still differed after matching (21% against 8.1%, P=0.01; 45.2% against 30.6%, P=0.001). Follow-up was 37.5 against 15.5 months after matching (P=0.006) and surveillance was asymmetric, with endoscopic patients routinely re-scoped and biopsied and surgical patients not, so the recurrence comparison is not a like-for-like one and no time-to-event analysis of recurrence is presented. The R0 comparison is between a fragmented endoscopic specimen and an intact surgical one read by local pathologists at 58 centres over 14 years with no central review, which structurally favours surgery. With 63 surgical patients, 6 cancers and 1 against 2 severe adverse events in the matched arms, the safety comparison has no power to detect the morbidity difference that drives the clinical choice. On neuroendocrine tumours, a 14-patient single-institution series — cited here from its abstract only, since the full text was not obtained — reported R0 in all 8 pancreatoduodenectomy patients against 75% of 6 transduodenal cases with nodal involvement reaching 88% in the resection group, and concluded that the transduodenal approach may provide an inadequate oncological resection and can understage these tumours.

opts.name: Pancreatoduodenectomy for a benign or premalignant lesion
opts.when: NCCN: if endoscopic removal is not possible, pancreatoduodenectomy can be performed; and patients with positive margins after ampullectomy can go on to pancreatoduodenectomy. Patients who have an adenoma resected by pancreatoduodenectomy do not need surveillance.
opts.pref: A high malignancy risk score, repeated failed endoscopic and transduodenal attempts, or Spigelman stage IV polyposis not suitable for endoscopic therapy. In the 127-patient multi-institutional series of non-familial periampullary adenomas taken to pancreatoduodenectomy, 59 (46.4%) proved malignant — so in a selected high-risk group this is often the correct cancer operation performed before the cancer was proven. The authors concede the selection plainly: every patient in that cohort had already been judged to need a Whipple, the true denominator including patients managed endoscopically or by transduodenal resection is unknown, and their own earlier single-centre figure was 29%.
opts.avoid: Do not use it as the default for a low-risk adenoma. In that same series the patients at no or low risk of malignancy had more major postoperative complications than the intermediate and high-risk groups, although across the three strata as defined the difference was not significant (51.7%, 27.1% and 29.4%, P=0.11) and reached significance only after the strata were collapsed at a score of 3 and adjusted (odds ratio 2.9, 95% CI 1.01–8.6, P=0.047); the published malignancy rates per stratum appear three different ways in the same paper. The quoted morbidity and mortality for pancreatoduodenectomy in ampullary disease are 27%–59% and 2%–10%, and the operation also carries a higher fistula risk here than in non-ampullary disease — clinically relevant fistula in 83 of 310 ampullary resections (26.8%) against 557 of 4,722 non-ampullary (11.8%), odds ratio 2.73 (95% CI 2.09–3.57), on a cross-dataset comparison rather than a within-cohort one.

standard.order: Ordered by proportionality to the demonstrated disease, not by survival — overall survival was comparable between the endoscopic and transduodenal routes in the only matched comparison, and no study compares transduodenal ampullectomy with pancreatoduodenectomy for benign disease in a way that controls selection. NCCN's own text is candid that the few direct comparisons of pancreatoduodenectomy and surgical ampullectomy contain too few ampullectomies to support a conclusion, and that attempts to establish standard indications for ampullectomy have not settled the criteria.
standard.flagnote: Ratification item: does this programme offer transduodenal ampullectomy at all, and under what written criteria? NCCN makes it conditional on local expertise and lists no indications, and the indication criteria remain undetermined in the literature. The European data do favour it over papillectomy on R0 and recurrence, but the matched analysis pairs 98.4% of the eligible surgical population with a 1-in-9 selection of the eligible endoscopic population, follow-up was more than twice as long in the surgical arm (37.5 against 15.5 months after matching, P=0.006), and endoscopic patients were routinely re-scoped with scar biopsies while surgical patients were not — so the recurrence gap is inflated by design. 36.6% of the surgical specimens held advanced cancer and 14.8% held no neoplasm at all. An operation offered without written criteria will be offered inconsistently. Audit: indication, final histology, R status, recurrence, reintervention.

alt.t: Pancreas-preserving duodenectomy in familial adenomatous polyposis with uncontrollable benign duodenal disease.
alt.pref: Spigelman stage IV disease without malignancy, where endoscopic therapy can no longer control the duodenum. Pancreatoduodenectomy is the operation when duodenal cancer is present, and an intraoperative frozen section can decide between them when malignancy is in doubt.
alt.avoid: Counsel against the morbidity honestly: reported in-hospital morbidity is 49% regardless of indication, with other series at 60%–76%, long-term pancreatitis 16%–21% and exocrine insufficiency 30%–60%, and 30-day mortality from 2% to 29%. Adenomas in the neo-duodenum are eventually found in 50%–78% of patients at a median of 46 to 75 months, so the operation does not end surveillance, and 3 of 47 patients (6.4%) in one series developed adenocarcinoma afterwards at a median of 9.25 years. All of these figures reach this page through a narrative review that reports them as unweighted ranges across series of 6 to 49 patients, with no protocol, no risk-of-bias appraisal and no pooling — use them to frame the conversation, not to quote a number.
alt.note: There is no long-term evidence that endoscopic therapy reduces cancer risk or prevents this operation. The review that sets this out is blunt about it: across 7 cohort studies published in a decade, totalling 181 polyposis patients, five reported residual or recurrent disease in 78%–100% of non-ampullary and 15%–38% of ampullary disease, one found that stage IV patients downstaged by endoscopic therapy subsequently progressed faster than patients with primary progression, and only one reported duodenal adenocarcinoma after endoscopic therapy at all. Its authors go as far as to suggest it may be time to reconsider the use of endoscopic therapy in these patients. That is why the choice belongs in a multidisciplinary discussion with the patient rather than in an algorithm. [EXPERTISE]

avoid.t: Do not perform a transduodenal ampullectomy for invasive carcinoma in order to avoid a pancreatoduodenectomy.
avoid.pref: If the lesion is an invasive adenocarcinoma, the operation is a pancreatoduodenectomy with regional lymphadenectomy — gate 5.
avoid.avoid: It cannot stage the nodes, and nodal status is the dominant prognostic variable: in 313 pathologically re-reviewed ampullary resections, median overall survival was 107.5 months for node-negative against 32 months for node-positive disease (P<0.0001), with 45% node positive on a median of 11 nodes examined. A National Cancer Database analysis of 8,127 resections, cited here from its abstract only because the full text was not obtained, reports lymph node metastasis in 56.7%. NCCN's own summary is that ampullectomy has lower morbidity and mortality but a higher recurrence rate, and the European comparison bears that out at the extreme: of 88 invasive cancers treated endoscopically, R0 was achieved in 30 (34.1%), and endotherapy alone succeeded in 34 of 75 T1a (45.3%) and 5 of 13 T1b cancers (38.5%) — it failed in roughly two-thirds of T1 disease.

gates.name: 5 · Pancreatoduodenectomy for invasive carcinoma
crit: Invasive ampullary adenocarcinoma, or a lesion whose malignancy risk makes a cancer operation correct
No peritoneal, hepatic or distant nodal metastases on staging or at operation
Patient fit for pancreatoduodenectomy with reconstruction
High-volume centre, with a pathologist briefed on orientation and margins
Biliary stent only where gate 0's indications were met
gates.ask: Can I take this out with a clear margin, harvest enough nodes to stage it honestly, and will the pathology report answer the adjuvant question?

standard.t: Pancreatoduodenectomy with standard regional lymphadenectomy, dissecting the SMA margin meticulously and treating margin status as the thing that is actually in your hands.
standard.pref: Every resectable invasive ampullary adenocarcinoma. NCCN's goals are an R0 resection with regional nodes, meticulous perivascular dissection as for pancreatic cancer, recognition of the need for venous resection and reconstruction, and intraoperative exclusion of peritoneal, liver and distant nodal disease. Reported 5-year survival after pancreatoduodenectomy for ampullary adenocarcinoma is 32% to 78%, with morbidity 27%–59% and mortality 2%–10%.
standard.avoid: Do not treat the margin as a reporting formality. In 313 ampullary resections, surgical margin positivity correlated with nodal stage (P=0.001). Under the CAP protocol tumour at or within 1 mm of a margin is a positive margin, but NCCN states plainly that this is extrapolated from rectal cancer data and that there is currently a lack of definitive evidence for what constitutes an adequate margin in ampullary resection specimens. NCCN suggests frozen section of the pancreatic neck and bile duct about 5 mm back from the transection to avoid cautery artefact, and further excision to achieve 5 mm of clearance if tumour is within that distance.
standard.note: Prognostic factors across series are lymphovascular invasion, perineural invasion, size and stage, ulceration, differentiation, nodal burden and margin status, but the data vary widely. Perineural invasion is the clearest of them in NCCN's own summary: median survival 18.7 against 51.9 months with and without it in 70 patients (P=0.001), and 5-year survival 36.8% against 72.1% in 89 patients (P<0.001). One ampullary-specific operative point from the multi-institutional adjuvant series is worth knowing before consent: ampullary pancreatoduodenectomy carried a higher fistula risk than non-ampullary, with a mean Fistula Risk Score of 4.3 against 3.6 and a soft gland in 73.9% against 52.9% (both P<0.001), and clinically relevant postoperative pancreatic fistula in 83 of 310 (26.8%) against 557 of 4,722 (11.8%), odds ratio 2.73 (95% CI 2.09–3.57) — a comparison made against a separate fistula-study dataset with no matching for era, centre or surgeon, so treat the direction as real and the magnitude as approximate. [EXPERTISE]

standard.t: Harvest and count the nodes, and report the number involved rather than only node-positive or node-negative.
standard.pref: Every resection. A National Cancer Database analysis of 8,127 ampullary resections placed the inflection point in the survival hazard at 20 examined nodes and concluded that a minimum of 20 is needed to stratify prognosis and minimise stage migration, with the log-odds nodal classification the most prognostic of the four schemes tested; that paper is cited here from its abstract only, because the full text was not obtained, so the derivation of the threshold cannot be inspected. PERIPAN, finding no ampullary-specific evidence, recommends adhering to the same minimum lymph node yield as for pancreatic cancer — where groups have proposed 11 to 17 as a quality indicator — until better data exist, and recommends revisiting the specimen and submitting more tissue when the count falls short.
standard.avoid: Do not read a low count as reassurance, and do not read nodal substaging as a settled gain. In 313 pathologically verified resections the median number of nodes examined was 11, only 150 (48%) had 12 or more, and 45% were node positive overall but 56% among those with 12 or more examined. Substaging by metastatic node number gave median survival of 107.5 months for N0, 40 months for one to two involved nodes and 24.5 months for three or more (P<0.0001), with 5-year survival 62%, 31.5% and 30% and adjusted hazard ratios of 1.6 (95% CI 1.1–2.4) and 1.9 (1.1–3.2), P for trend 0.018 — a modest effect whose lower confidence bounds nearly touch 1. The N1 and N2 5-year estimates are essentially identical, which is the comparison clinicians actually use. AJCC 8th edition uses one to three and four or more as its N1 and N2 boundaries.
standard.note: Two findings from the full text of that nodal series change how it should be quoted. First, the clean N0-versus-N1 separation does not survive adequate sampling: restricted to the 150 patients with 12 or more nodes examined, median survival was not reached for N0, 74 months for N1 and 29 months for N2 (P=0.02) with 5-year survival 64%, 52% and 38% — the N0 and N1 curves converge, which implies that part of the apparent value of substaging in the whole cohort comes from understaging in the half with fewer than 12 nodes. The authors note the convergence and still recommend the scheme. Second, adjuvant therapy data were not available at all, and node-positive patients are precisely those most likely to have received chemotherapy, so the N1 and N2 hazard ratios are confounded by treatment in an unknown direction. N2 cases were also markedly over-represented at the one institution using a different gross dissection method (26% against 13.5%), so the N1/N2 split is partly a marker of which laboratory handled the specimen. Nodal risk rises steeply with T stage in the series NCCN tabulates — 28.0%, 50.9%, 71.7% and 77.3% for T1 to T4 in one of 450 patients, and 11.3%, 28.4%, 43.8% and 100% in another of 259 — which is also why a papillectomy for invasive disease leaves a real question unanswered.

alt.t: Neoadjuvant systemic therapy, with or without subsequent chemoradiation, in a patient with high-risk features — presented as a selection exercise, not as a survival benefit.
alt.pref: NCCN's high-risk features are equivocal or indeterminate imaging findings, markedly elevated CA 19-9 or CEA, large primary tumours, large regional nodes, excessive weight loss and extreme pain. Regimens differ by presumed subtype: CapeOx, FOLFIRINOX or FOLFOX for intestinal type; albumin-bound paclitaxel–gemcitabine, capecitabine–gemcitabine, cisplatin–gemcitabine or FOLFIRINOX for pancreatobiliary and mixed type. Repeat pancreatic-protocol CT or MRI afterwards, then operate if still resectable.
alt.avoid: Do not offer it as a treatment effect. In the largest series NCCN cites — 8,688 ampullary cancers with 175 receiving neoadjuvant therapy — median overall survival was 43 against 33 months with surgery first and the difference was not significant (P=0.416), and the neoadjuvant patients were younger and more often node-positive. Neoadjuvant use runs at only 1%–4% of resections, downstaging occurred in 15%–67% of tumours, and NCCN states there is limited evidence to recommend specific neoadjuvant regimens off-study and that there are no prospective randomised phase III data behind these recommendations. Name the borrowing when you offer a regimen: modified FOLFIRINOX comes from PRODIGE-24, a trial of resected pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma that excluded nonductal pancreatic tumours by design, restricted entry to WHO performance status 0–1, age under 80 and CA 19-9 under 180 U/mL, and produced grade 3 or 4 toxicity in 75.9% of patients — with no disease-free survival benefit in the 101 patients aged 70 or over (hazard ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.53–1.39), who are closer to the median age of ampullary cancer than the trial population as a whole.
alt.note: Surgery first is NCCN's preferred route for resectable disease. Where chemoradiation is considered because of positive or close margins, chemotherapy should be given before it. Nothing in the adjuvant pancreatic trials transfers to the neoadjuvant ampullary setting: PRODIGE-24 enrolled only after complete macroscopic resection, excluded nonductal tumours, and reported in a disease whose resected median survival is roughly half that of ampullary cancer. [PROTOCOL]

alt.t: Minimally invasive pancreatoduodenectomy where the programme does them.
alt.pref: NCCN records that meta-analysis and a multicentre international cohort found better operative time, blood loss and length of stay with laparoscopic than open pancreatoduodenectomy.
alt.avoid: NCCN also states that how laparoscopic and robotic pancreatoduodenectomy compare with the open operation remains to be investigated, and the ampullary-specific data are thin. Approach is a programme decision about volume and expertise, not an oncological one. [EXPERTISE]

avoid.t: Do not add an extended lymphadenectomy.
avoid.pref: Standard regional lymphadenectomy, with the nodes counted. Mark and submit separately any station taken beyond the standard dissection, as PERIPAN asks.
avoid.avoid: In the pancreatic literature, which NCCN carries across to this operation, a randomised single-institution trial, an Italian multicentre randomised series of 81 patients, a Japanese randomised multicentre trial and multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomised trials all found no survival impact from extended lymphadenectomy, with more postoperative diarrhoea. Sampling of aortocaval and common hepatic artery nodes can be considered because involvement there carries an inferior prognosis — that is staging, not therapy.
avoid.note: Downgraded from A to B. The randomised evidence against extended lymphadenectomy is strong, consistent and large, but all of it is in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma; no randomised trial of lymphadenectomy extent has been done in ampullary cancer, and the extrapolation is NCCN's. Grade A on an ampullary page would claim randomised ampullary evidence that does not exist. The recommendation itself is not in doubt, and the direction of any residual uncertainty favours the standard operation.

avoid.t: Do not route a locally advanced tumour to a resection attempt without a second opinion.
avoid.pref: NCCN treats locally advanced ampullary disease the same way as metastatic disease in the current version, and asks for referral to a tertiary cancer centre for a second opinion about unresectability — that is gate 7 from here.
avoid.avoid: An exploratory attempt that violates the tumour plane converts a systemic-therapy patient into a systemic-therapy patient with a laparotomy.

gates.name: 6 · Histologic subtype, mismatch repair and molecular testing
crit: Subtype assigned on the invasive component, not on the precursor lesion
Mixed subtype used only when the lesser component is at least 30% of the tumour
Tubular-NOS used where a confident call cannot be made, with the favoured lineage stated
Mismatch-repair testing done as a reflex, independent of subtype
Somatic profiling where metastatic disease and anticancer therapy are both in prospect
gates.ask: Is this subtype call reliable enough to choose an adjuvant regimen off it, and has anyone sent the mismatch-repair test?

standard.t: Report the subtype as intestinal, pancreatobiliary, mixed or tubular-NOS, based on the invasive component and on morphology, with immunohistochemistry as support rather than as the determinant.
standard.pref: Every resected invasive ampullary carcinoma. PERIPAN asks for subtyping of tubular-type adenocarcinomas based on the invasive component, reserving mixed for tumours with unequivocal intestinal and pancreatobiliary areas where the lesser component is at least 30%, and replacing the old term hybrid with tubular-NOS, with the favoured lineage and component percentages given in a comment. NCCN asks for intestinal, pancreatobiliary or mixed, with ambiguous cases classified as tubular adenocarcinoma with mixed features and the predominant pattern noted.
standard.avoid: Do not rely on an immunohistochemical panel to settle it. NCCN states that immunohistochemistry is not required and that overlap between intestinal and pancreatobiliary profiles may make current panels unreliable for definitive determination. PERIPAN adds that pancreatobiliary tumours are more likely to express MUC1 and CK7 and less likely CDX2, MUC2 and CK20 — and the reverse for intestinal — but that none of these markers is entirely specific or sensitive individually or in combination, that studies have used positivity thresholds of 1%, 5%, 10%, 20% and 50%, and that even the best-performing published formula leaves more than a quarter of cases ambiguous.
standard.note: Typical morphology: intestinal tumours have large tubules lined by tall columnar cells with elongated, pseudostratified, hyperchromatic nuclei, with dirty intraluminal necrosis as a further clue; pancreatobiliary tumours have more widely separated, smaller, simpler glands lined by cuboidal or low columnar cells without stratification, often with desmoplastic stroma.

standard.t: State the reproducibility of the subtype call alongside the call itself — interobserver agreement is fair, not good.
standard.pref: Any report or board discussion where the subtype is about to drive a treatment choice. In 232 resected ampullary carcinomas with an invasive component over 3.0 mm, read independently and blind by five pathologists from five institutions, overall agreement on a purist four-category scheme was fair (κ 0.39, P<0.001) and all five observers agreed in 53 of 232 cases (23%). By consensus of three of five the commonest category was mixed pancreatobiliary-intestinal at 94 cases (40%), then pure pancreatobiliary 74 (32%), other 51 (22%) and pure intestinal only 13 (6%). Asked to force each tumour into a predominant pattern, agreement improved only to moderate (κ 0.44, P<0.0001) with all five agreeing in 81 cases (35%).
standard.avoid: Do not present the prognostic claim without this, because the claim exists only under the forced classification. Under the purist scheme there was no survival difference at all: pure intestinal 80 against pure pancreatobiliary 40 months (P=0.33), and across pure pancreatobiliary, mixed and pure intestinal 40, 56 and 80 months (P=0.65), with T stage, node status and 3- and 5-year survival all non-significant. Only after the 94 indeterminate mixed tumours — 40% of the cohort — were force-assigned to a side did a difference appear: pancreatobiliary-predominant against intestinal-predominant median survival 41 against 80 months (P=0.026), 3-year 55% against 75%, 5-year 38% against 57%, hazard ratio for death 1.78 (95% CI 1.06–2.98, P=0.028). And that difference was not independent: on multivariable analysis high tumour budding, high T stage and node positivity all remained significant while predominant histologic type failed, P=0.39. NCCN's own position is that current data on the independent prognostic and predictive value of subtyping are conflicting. PERIPAN says the role of immunohistochemistry and tumour markers in prognosis or treatment response is still unclear, and attributes that to the inconsistent definitions of ampullary carcinoma used in the historical literature.
standard.note: The mixed phenotype is a feature of the organ, not a failure of the pathologist: the ampulla sits at the junction of three epithelia, and intratumoral heterogeneity is expected. That is also why the subtype in a biopsy may not be the subtype in the tumour. Two details make the 23% full-agreement figure an optimistic ceiling rather than a floor.
