honest.t: The whole page is built around the assumption that a biopsy reading adenoma should be treated as potentially harbouring carcinoma, and that the operation should be chosen on a risk estimate rather than on the biopsy.
honest.why: Grade C. The false-negative rate is well documented (20%–40% per NCCN, 20%–30% per PERIPAN, 8 of 90 biopsy–resection pairs a benign biopsy with a malignant resection, 32% occult carcinoma in papillectomies done for lesions judged benign, 46.4% malignancy in a surgical series selected for resection) and a risk score exists, but no study randomises management strategy against biopsy result, the score has never been externally validated, and each of the supporting figures comes from a cohort selected in a way that shifts it. The position is defensible and it is not an evidence-based threshold.

honest.t: No numeric threshold is given here for when a malignancy risk score should push a patient from papillectomy to pancreatoduodenectomy.
honest.why: Deliberate. The published score stratifies malignancy risk at 10.3%, 44.1% and 88.2% but says nothing about which operation each stratum should get, publishes three mutually inconsistent sets of those numbers, was never validated outside its derivation cohort, and was built entirely in patients who had already had a pancreatoduodenectomy. The same paper shows the lowest-risk group has the highest major-complication odds, most plausibly because an unobstructed gland is soft. A cut-off here would be an institutional convention dressed as evidence. It belongs in approvals, not in the gate.

honest.t: The histologic subtype is reported and used, while its interobserver agreement is κ 0.39 and its prognostic effect is not independent of stage.
honest.why: This is the page's most uncomfortable position and it is deliberately stated twice. The full-text read made it worse rather than better. In the reproducibility study, five blinded observers reached κ 0.39 with full agreement in 23% of 232 cases, 40% of tumours were mixed and pure intestinal morphology was present in only 6%; the survival difference between subtypes appeared only after the mixed cases were force-assigned to a side, and even then failed multivariable analysis at P=0.39 while budding, T stage and nodes survived. NCCN's own discussion calls the prognostic and predictive data conflicting; PERIPAN calls the role of markers unclear and attributes that to inconsistent historical definitions of the disease. We report the subtype because the guidelines organise the regimen lists around it, not because the call is reliable or because it has been shown to predict anything independently.

honest.t: Whether adjuvant therapy should be offered preferentially to pancreatobiliary and mixed subtypes is genuinely unresolved, and the page does not pick a side.
honest.why: The two cohorts are not of equal methodological weight, and the page should not present them as a coin toss. The positive study (214 European resections) gave adjuvant therapy by tumour-board decision on T3/4 stage, node positivity and CA 19-9, performed no propensity matching, weighting or landmark analysis, reported no interaction test, pooled its 16 mixed tumours with pancreatobiliary after seeing the data, and reports a whole-cohort result running the other way (median overall survival 168 months without adjuvant therapy against 113 months with it, hazard ratio 1.124, 95% CI 0.756–1.987, P=0.608) together with several hazard ratios that lie outside their own confidence limits and a whole-cohort median survival of 136.5 months far outside every other series. The negative study (357 resections, 81 propensity-matched pairs) matched on the factors that actually drove treatment selection, excluded 90-day deaths to limit immortal time bias, and found the signal absent in both subtypes and at every stage stratum. So the better-controlled analysis is negative. What it is not is decisive: its intervals do not exclude a 25% to 35% relative risk reduction, half the screened population was excluded for unknown subtype, and misclassification of a κ-0.39 variable biases any subtype interaction towards the null. ESPAC-3 could not settle it — only 135 of its 297 ampullary tumours could be subtyped at all, leaving 80 intestinal and 46 pancreatobiliary split across three arms, with no interaction test and no power calculation. A third retrospective series found benefit confined to the intestinal subtype. The page does not pick a side on whether to treat by subtype, but it no longer presents the two cohorts as equally informative.

honest.t: ESPAC-3 was never powered for its ampullary subgroup and reports no hypothesis test for ampullary-only survival anywhere, so this page cannot cite it as establishing adjuvant benefit in ampullary cancer.
honest.why: This is the single most important correction the full-text read produced. The trial was powered on 243 deaths and 430 patients to detect a 12 percentage-point absolute 5-year gain across the pooled periampullary population, and its authors state that a separate analysis for each tumour type could not be built into the design. Within the 297 ampullary patients the medians are observation 40.6 months (95% CI 30.6–61.4, 59 deaths), fluorouracil 57.8 months (32.8–84.0, 50 deaths) and gemcitabine 70.8 months (45.3–not estimable, 42 deaths), and they appear with no P value because none was computed. The primary analysis across all 428 patients was negative (hazard ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.66–1.11, P=0.25) and became significant only after multivariable adjustment (0.75, 0.57–0.98, P=0.03) for age, bile duct histology, poor differentiation and node positivity — and the observation arm was prognostically the worst at baseline on two of those four (poorly differentiated 33% against 22% and 19%; node positive 62% against 60% and 54%), so the shift partly corrects a randomisation imbalance rather than independently confirming the result. Quoting the ampullary medians alone is the most favourable possible framing of this trial, and the page says so wherever it quotes them. Adjuvant chemotherapy is still offered, because the adjusted estimate and the registry data point the same way and because there is nothing better; it is offered as a reasonable choice, not as a demonstrated benefit.

honest.t: The extracted NCCN systemic-therapy page overstates ESPAC-3 and carries figures that appear to belong to a different trial cohort.
honest.why: It states that ESPAC-3 demonstrated significant improvements in disease-free and overall survival with adjuvant gemcitabine or fluorouracil versus observation in resectable ampullary adenocarcinoma, and quotes median survivals of 23.0 and 23.6 months for fluorouracil–leucovorin and gemcitabine. The published periampullary trial reported neither — its primary analysis was negative and its ampullary medians are 57.8 and 70.8 months; those 23-month figures match the ESPAC-3 pancreatic cohort. The full-text read confirms the discrepancy from the trial side: there is no significant disease-free or overall survival result for ampullary adenocarcinoma in ESPAC-3 to report, adjusted or otherwise, because the subgroup was never tested. The guideline's own discussion section states the position correctly. This needs checking against the published PDF before the page is ratified, and is flagged in nonpm.

honest.t: Preoperative biliary stenting is discouraged on the strength of a randomised trial in pancreatic head cancer, not in ampullary tumours.
honest.why: Grade C after the full-text read, down from B, and the extrapolation is larger than it first looks. The effect was large on the composite endpoint (serious complications within 120 days 39% against 74%, relative risk 0.54, 95% CI 0.41–0.71) but the composite counts drainage complications and surgical complications in one tally, and surgical complications alone did not differ (37% against 47%, relative risk 0.79, 0.57–1.11, P=0.14) — so on the question clinicians actually ask, the trial is null. The intervention was a 10 Fr plastic stent left 4 to 6 weeks, with cholangitis in 26% and a need for exchange in 30%, and the authors themselves recommend metal stents for the neoadjuvant setting, which concedes that what was tested is not what is now used. Site was carried only as a pancreatic-versus-periampullary covariate with no ampullary subgroup reported, 92% of patients had adenocarcinoma of the pancreatic head, only 61% went on to resection, and the palliative-bypass subgroup drove much of the difference. NCCN states the position; nobody has tested it in ampullary tumours.

honest.t: The prophylactic pancreatic duct stent is treated as standard on the basis of one randomised trial of 19 patients.
honest.why: Grade C after the full-text read, down from B, and fragile in fact. The 19-patient trial was stopped early at a pre-specified interim look triggered by a 30% event rate in the control arm, against a planned 25 per arm, and reports three results from the same data: 33% against 0% as treated (P=0.02), 25% against 0% excluding the failed placement (P=0.05), and 25% against 9% by intention to treat, where significance is lost (P=0.3). Its outcome window was 24 hours. The 45-patient randomised comparison of wire-guided against conventional technique missed its primary endpoint (pancreatitis 18% against 13%, P=0.960) despite achieving stent placement in 100% against 65%, and its much-quoted internal finding of 37.5% pancreatitis when stenting failed against 0% when it succeeded is a post-randomisation comparison between patients who differ by procedural difficulty. ESGE grades prophylactic stenting strong on moderate-quality evidence; the underlying randomised evidence is 64 patients and 10 events. The recommendation stands on consistency of direction and on a cheap, reversible intervention, not on trial precision.

honest.t: Whether this programme offers transduodenal surgical ampullectomy at all, and on what criteria, is left open.
honest.why: NCCN makes it conditional on local expertise and lists no indications. The best comparative data — 62 propensity-matched pairs from a 1,673-patient European database — favour it over papillectomy on R0 (90.3% against 72.6%, P=0.02) and recurrence, with comparable survival, but the full-text read shows the comparison is built in a way that favours it. The 62 pairs are 98.4% of the eligible surgical patients and only 10.9% of the eligible papillectomy patients, so the surgical arm is its whole population while the endoscopic arm is a 1-in-9 selection chosen to resemble it; matching omitted intraductal extension, duct dilation and index-session ablation, and intrabiliary extension and duct dilation still differed afterwards; follow-up was 37.5 against 15.5 months after matching (P=0.006); and endoscopic patients were routinely re-scoped with scar biopsies while surgical patients were not, so the fivefold recurrence gap conflates residual disease with differential ascertainment. The surgical arm has 63 patients and 6 cancers, the only procedure-related death in the study is in it, and 36.6% of its specimens held advanced cancer while 14.8% held no neoplasm. The one unambiguous finding is burden: 227.5 against 30 minutes and 14 against 3 hospital days. An operation offered without written criteria is offered inconsistently.

honest.t: What to do with an invasive carcinoma found incidentally in a margin-negative papillectomy specimen in a fit patient is not resolved here.
honest.why: NCCN routes it to pancreatoduodenectomy. The propensity-matched multicentre cohort that is used to argue otherwise found no overall survival difference between papillectomy alone and papillectomy plus surgery (89.2% against 82.3% at 5 years, P=0.861), but its recurrence endpoints missed significance twice in the same direction — matched recurrence-free survival 66.1% against 86.7% at P=0.052, and 61.4% against 82.6% at P=0.066 in the adenocarcinoma-only subgroup — on 55 matched patients. It never reports T stage, which is the variable the whole question turns on, since T1b carries a substantially higher nodal metastasis risk than T1a; nodal status is unknown in the papillectomy arm by definition; and the immortal time the surgical arm had to survive to enter it is unaddressed, biasing overall survival towards surgery and against the paper's own conclusion. Neither answer is evidence-based; the group needs one position rather than one per endoscopist, and the position should specify what happens when T1a and T1b cannot be distinguished.

honest.t: Surveillance after papillectomy is set at at least 5 years, and the page does not say when it stops.
honest.why: ESGE's wording is at least 5 years and its month-by-month schedule carries no derivation, no interval-cancer analysis and no burden assessment. Recurrence after a histological R0 was still 13% at 5 years in 798 Japanese patients, which is the honest reason to keep going. The ten-year argument is weaker than it reads: it comes from one cohort whose mean follow-up (2.8 years) was shorter than its own mean time to recurrence (3.2 years), whose single latest event at 9.75 years drives the recommendation, and whose internal stratifications show more recurrence after en bloc than piecemeal resection and after initially complete than incomplete resection — the signature of early residual disease being classified out of the recurrence count. There is no study of stopping rules and no competing-risk analysis in this population. Setting an endpoint locally is reasonable; claiming evidence for it is not.

honest.t: In polyposis the page tells you not to biopsy duodenal lesions routinely, and in sporadic disease it tells you the biopsy is essential.
honest.why: Both are correct and the reason is base rates, not inconsistency. ESGE discourages routine duodenal biopsy in polyposis because it compromises optical diagnosis and future endoscopic mucosal resection, and because ampullary biopsy carries a pancreatitis risk; in a sporadic ampullary lesion the biopsy is the only thing standing between an adenoma plan and a cancer. The page states both rules and names the populations, because the commonest way to misapply either is to carry it across.

honest.t: The tumour board operating model and the audit items are operational requirements, not evidence-based interventions.
honest.why: Grade D by construction. They are listed as Standard because the programme would be choosing them, not because trials support them, and they should be audited for adherence rather than for effectiveness.

honest.t: ESPAC-4 and PRODIGE-24 sit in this depot as borrowed evidence from a different disease, and the page now says so wherever it uses them.
honest.why: Both are trials of resected pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma in which nonductal pancreatic tumours were an explicit exclusion criterion, so neither reports a single ampullary patient and neither can be read as evidence in this disease. ESPAC-4 gained 2.5 months of median survival (28.0 against 25.5 months, hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.68–0.98, P=0.032), was reported early at 458 of a planned 480 deaths with no alpha adjustment presented, and its benefit sat in R0 patients with essentially no separation in R1 disease. PRODIGE-24 doubled median disease-free survival (21.6 against 12.8 months) in a population restricted to performance status 0–1, age under 80 and CA 19-9 under 180 U/mL, at the cost of grade 3–4 toxicity in 75.9% of patients, and showed no disease-free survival benefit in the fifth of patients aged 70 or over (hazard ratio 0.86, 0.53–1.39) — the group closest to the median age of ampullary cancer. Ampullary carcinoma has roughly double the resected median survival of pancreatic cancer and no randomised evidence that any adjuvant chemotherapy helps, so transplanting these regimens is a decision about risk tolerance rather than an application of trial evidence. NCCN itself says the panel added capecitabine–gemcitabine on the basis of clinical expertise and that no prospective randomised phase III data support these recommendations.

honest.t: Roughly a third of both papillectomies and surgical ampullectomies in the largest European series were performed for the wrong indication, and that is a bigger problem than which operation is better.
honest.why: Final histology was neither adenoma nor adenocarcinoma — mostly hyperplastic or chronic inflammatory tissue — in 270 of 1,115 papillectomy patients (24.2%) and 25 of 169 surgical ampullectomy patients (14.8%), while advanced cancer (T2 or above, or node positive) was found in 122 papillectomy (10.9%) and 62 surgical ampullectomy (36.6%) patients. So in roughly a third of cases in each arm there was either no neoplasm to remove or disease already beyond what a local resection can treat. The authors call the rate of poor indications still high for both operations. Nothing on this page reduces that rate except the gate 0 and gate 1 discipline: a side-viewing examination, staged before any stent, with the compartment named and the malignancy risk stated out loud.

honest.t: The papillectomy R0 rate of 80% is closer to 66% once ablation at the index session is counted honestly, and papillectomy failed in roughly two-thirds of T1 cancers.
honest.why: In the European series, R0 for adenoma after papillectomy was 386 of 481 (80.2%); but 69 of those cases (14.4%) had argon plasma coagulation or radiofrequency ablation during the index procedure, which means visible residual tissue, and counting them as probable R2 resections brings the primary success rate of papillectomy alone to 317 of 481 (65.9%). Both figures appear in the paper without a preferred estimate, and the reclassification is the authors' retrospective assumption. Retreatment then cascades: of 40 adenoma patients given endoscopic retherapy, 17 (42.5%) were still incomplete at the next follow-up and 12 of the remaining 15 (80%) needed a third session. In invasive disease the failure is starker — of 88 T1 cancers treated endoscopically, R0 was achieved in 30 (34.1%), and endotherapy alone succeeded in 34 of 75 T1a (45.3%) and 5 of 13 T1b cancers (38.5%). Independently, in 798 Japanese papillectomies only 416 (52.1%) were R0 at all, and only 58.6% of technically successful en bloc resections were ultimately R0.

honest.t: The recurrence rates quoted after papillectomy are not measuring the same thing, so the page gives the definitions alongside the numbers.
honest.why: The 798-patient Japanese cohort counted any histologically confirmed neoplastic tissue with no requirement for a prior negative surveillance endoscopy, and its median time to recurrence was 6 months (3 months after R1), so a large fraction of its 18.3% is residual disease. The 136-patient single-centre cohort required one negative surveillance endoscopy first and allowed multiple treatment sessions inside its definition of complete eradication, which converts early incomplete resection into a non-event and shifts the curve rightwards — and its own data show the consequence, with more recurrence after en bloc (19.4%) than piecemeal (7.0%) resection and after initially complete (16.5%) than incomplete (6.1%) resection. A third cohort split recurrence into early and late by the timing of a first surveillance endoscopy left to the endoscopist's discretion, and publishes inconsistent denominators for both. The clinically useful statement is that about one in five patients will need further endoscopic treatment of the papilla; the precise rate depends on a definition nobody has standardised.

honest.t: An indeterminate resection margin is the commonest ambiguous pathology result in this pathway and no guideline says what to do about it.
honest.why: In the 798-patient Japanese cohort an Rx margin accounted for 206 specimens (25.8%), carried a hazard ratio of 2.38 for recurrence against R0 (95% CI 1.49–3.81) close to the 2.95 for a frankly positive margin, and by 5 years had the same cumulative recurrence as R1 at 34% — so it behaves like an undetected positive margin. ESGE offers no recommendation for it. Margin assessment in that study was local at 22 centres with no central review and no interobserver data, which is an argument for writing the local method down rather than for discounting the finding. This page's answer is to treat Rx as positive for surveillance purposes and to prevent it at the specimen-handling step, but that is a convention, not evidence.

honest.t: The one-in-six figure for mismatch-repair deficiency in ampullary carcinoma is the upper end of a wide range, not an established prevalence.
honest.why: PERIPAN's reflex-testing recommendation is graded low evidence and rests on an assertion that deficiency rates are comparable to colorectal cancer. The two primary series in this depot give 18 of 119 tested non-medullary ampullary carcinomas (15%), where the 119 were a convenience subset of 348 that happened to have been tested, and 1 of 23 early-onset ampullary carcinomas (4.3%) in a nationwide Dutch series whose signal was overwhelmingly in duodenal cancer (11 of 23, 47.8%). The claim that deficiency in ampullary cancer reliably indicates a hereditary defect rests, in that series, on one patient. None of this argues against reflex testing — the test is cheap, it does not depend on the unreliable subtype call, and it is simultaneously a treatment test and a germline trigger — but the programme should measure its own deficiency rate rather than quote one in six.

honest.t: The Spigelman score has never been validated, and the ampullary surveillance intervals that correct it are uncited panel judgement.
honest.why: The score was constructed in 1989 from a single cross-sectional screening round of 102 polyposis patients, with its four components and cut-points assigned from known risk factors rather than derived from any cancer outcome; no patient in that paper developed duodenal cancer during the study, and no formal validation has appeared since. Its components are equally weighted without rationale, its stage boundaries are arbitrary breaks in a 4-to-12-point range, and two of the four require histology that current guidelines discourage obtaining — so the stage as now computed is not the quantity the score was built from. The best supporting cohort found high-grade dysplasia in 5 of 8 stage IV patients (reported as 4 of 8 elsewhere in the same paper) and none at stages 0, II or III, but had one incident invasive cancer in total, no patients at stage I, and a protocol that left small and ampullary lesions unbiopsied and scored them at floor values, so stage assignment and outcome were not independent. The ESGE and BSG ampullary intervals of 5, 3 and 1 year are described in the guideline as proposed intervals that seem safe, with no citation and no modelling. The page keeps both because about half of duodenal cancers in these patients are periampullary and the alternative is nothing; it grades them D.

honest.t: Five papers cited on this page were not obtained in full text and are quoted from their abstracts only.
honest.why: They are the National Cancer Database node-yield analysis (PMID 38353072), which supplies the 20-node threshold and the 56.7% nodal metastasis rate; the intraductal ultrasound and transpapillary biopsy series (22319960), which supplies the 68.7% forceps sensitivity and the 97% combined figure; the 91-patient malignancy prediction cohort (23442830), which supplies the 26.4% malignancy rate and its odds ratios; the EUS preoperative evaluation series (30834717), which supplies the 120-patient T- and N-stage accuracy figures; and the 14-patient ampullary neuroendocrine tumour series (27457864), which supplies the R0 and nodal figures behind the warning against transduodenal resection of those tumours. Their selection, blinding, reference standards and stated limitations could not be checked, so every string that uses them says so. BILCAP (30922733) and ABC-02 (20375404) are likewise quoted from abstract and guideline text only; both are trials in other diseases.

honest.t: The grades on this page fell in several places after the full-text read, and every downgrade is explained in the note on the string it belongs to.
honest.why: Preoperative biliary drainage moved from B to C (borrowed population, composite endpoint, null surgical-complication result, plastic stents only); prophylactic pancreatic stenting from B to C (64 randomised patients, one trial negative on intention to treat, the other on its primary endpoint); adjuvant chemotherapy for stage II and III disease from B to C (the only randomised trial was negative on its primary endpoint and never tested its ampullary subgroup); extended lymphadenectomy from A to B (the randomised evidence is strong but entirely in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma); adjuvant chemoradiation from C to D (all registry and retrospective with treatment allocated by the factors adjusted for, and the best-adjusted cohort analysis negative); the malignancy risk score from C to D (derived and tested in the same already-resected cohort, three inconsistent sets of published strata); papillectomy with surveillance for an incidental early carcinoma from C to D (55 matched patients, T stage never reported, immortal time bias unaddressed); transduodenal ampullectomy from C to D (63 surgical patients, 1-in-9 matched selection, unequal follow-up and asymmetric surveillance); rare non-tubular subtypes from C to D (11 medullary cases, no blinded review, selective marker availability); first-line systemic therapy in metastatic disease from C to D (not one listed regimen has been tested in a trial reporting an ampullary population); and polyposis surveillance intervals from C to D (an unvalidated score and uncited intervals). No recommendation was removed. The roadmap's positions stand; what changed is how well supported the page says they are.

board: Submission — the form captures the endoscopic compartment (ampullary-duodenal, intra-ampullary, ampullary-ductal), lesion size, biopsy result with the number and site of biopsies, bile and pancreatic duct calibre, symptoms, age, EUS and MRCP findings including intraductal extension as a length, polyposis status, and the clinical question. Owner: submitting clinician.

Triage — a coordinator and a clinically trained gatekeeper check whether the imaging and endoscopic package is complete enough to decide between an endoscopic and an open operation, and whether a side-viewing examination has actually been done. Incomplete packages are returned rather than discussed. Owners: coordinator and chair.

Attendance — advanced endoscopy and hepatobiliary or pancreatic surgery must both be present for any benign-end case, because the decision is between their two operations. Pathology, diagnostic radiology, medical oncology, radiation oncology, genetic counselling and coordination attend; a dietitian is available. Owners: specialty leads.

Pathology — pre-alerted for every papillectomy and ampullectomy specimen, with orientation and margins agreed in writing before the specimen is sent, and the specimen reaching the department fresh and fixed within about 30 minutes. Specimens are not opened by non-pathology staff. Owner: pathology.

The benign-end rule — every case where the biopsy reads adenoma is discussed with an explicit malignancy risk estimate stated out loud, and the recommendation records which operation was chosen and why the other was not. Owner: chair.

Reflex tests — mismatch-repair testing is ordered on every ampullary carcinoma at diagnosis without needing a request, and germline testing is offered to every patient with confirmed ampullary adenocarcinoma or a relevant family history. Owners: pathology and genetic counselling.

Subtype discussion — the pathology report states the subtype on the invasive component with the percentage of any lesser component, and the board records whether the subtype changed the adjuvant recommendation. Owner: pathology.

Polyposis lane — polyposis patients are discussed with both the Spigelman stage and the ampullary appearance stated, and the interval set to the shorter of the two. A named polyposis owner holds the recall. Owner: polyposis lead.

Output — one recommendation, one owner, one due date, one reassessment date, one documented alternative considered, and the surveillance schedule named before the patient leaves the meeting. Owner: chair.

Documentation and registry — a note within one business day in the agreed structured format, and the case closed in the registry with the decision, the operation delivered, the final histology, R status and node count, and the outcome at reassessment. Owners: named owner and coordinator.

Referring relationships — the referring clinician is told the recommendation and who owns the next step. Patients are returned with a plan; community relationships are protected explicitly. Owner: named owner.
dashboard: For every papillectomy: en bloc versus piecemeal, R status reported as R0, R1 or Rx with the local reason for any Rx, whether argon plasma coagulation or radiofrequency ablation was used at the index session (recorded separately from R status), prophylactic pancreatic stent placed or not, and pancreatitis, bleeding and perforation.
Final histology against preoperative biopsy for every resected ampullary lesion — the local false-negative rate for invasive carcinoma, measured rather than assumed.
Malignancy risk score recorded at the board against final histology, by operation chosen.

Recurrence after papillectomy by margin status including Rx, with time to recurrence, reported both counting and excluding disease found at the first surveillance endoscopy, out to at least 5 years and not truncated at 2.
Surveillance adherence after papillectomy: proportion with a documented duodenoscopy and scar biopsy at 3, 6 and 12 months and annually thereafter.
Pancreatoduodenectomy: annual volume, 90-day mortality, R0 rate, and the number of lymph nodes examined per specimen against the programme's stated minimum.
Proportion of resections with a subtype assigned on the invasive component, and the proportion reported as mixed or tubular-NOS.
Proportion of resections with a subtype assigned on the invasive component, the proportion reported as mixed or tubular-NOS, and whether the subtype changed the adjuvant recommendation.
Mismatch-repair testing completion rate on resected ampullary carcinoma, with the local deficiency rate measured rather than compared against an assumed one in six, and germline referrals generated.
Adjuvant therapy: uptake by stage and subtype, regimen and its documented evidence source, start within 12 weeks, completion, toxicity and recurrence site.
Polyposis cohort: proportion with a documented ampullary appearance at each surveillance endoscopy, interval achieved against interval set, and non-attendance rate.

Indication quality at the benign end: for every papillectomy and surgical ampullectomy, the proportion whose final histology was neither adenoma nor adenocarcinoma, and the proportion found to have T2 or above or node-positive disease — the two halves of the roughly one-in-three wrong-indication rate reported in the European series.

For every T1 ampullary adenocarcinoma treated locally: T substage where assessable, R status, whether completion pancreatoduodenectomy followed, and recurrence — against the 34.1% R0 rate for endoscopic treatment of T1 disease in the European series.

approvals.q: What malignancy risk, on a stated score, moves a biopsy-proven ampullary adenoma from papillectomy to pancreatoduodenectomy?
approvals.why: The published score stratifies malignancy risk at 10.3%, 44.1% and 88.2% but assigns no operation to any stratum, publishes three mutually inconsistent sets of those proportions, was derived and tested in the same 127 patients with no validation statistic of any kind, and was built entirely in patients already judged to need a pancreatoduodenectomy. In the same series the lowest-risk patients had the most major complications. There is no threshold in the literature to adopt, and the programme should decide whether it uses the score as a structured conversation or as a number.
approvals.audit: Score recorded at the board against final histology and against major complications, by operation chosen.

approvals.q: Does the programme offer transduodenal surgical ampullectomy, and under what written criteria?
approvals.why: NCCN makes it conditional on local expertise and lists no indications; the indication criteria remain undetermined in the literature. The comparative data favour it over papillectomy on R0 (90.3% against 72.6%) and recurrence but come from 62 propensity-matched pairs in which the surgical arm is 98.4% of its eligible population and the endoscopic arm a 1-in-9 selection, follow-up was 37.5 against 15.5 months, and only the endoscopic patients were systematically re-scoped with scar biopsies. 36.6% of the surgical specimens held advanced cancer. The reliable difference is burden: 227.5 against 30 minutes and 14 against 3 days. [EXPERTISE]
approvals.audit: Indication, final histology, R status, recurrence and reintervention for every case.

approvals.q: An invasive carcinoma found incidentally in a margin-negative papillectomy specimen in a fit patient — complete to pancreatoduodenectomy, or surveil? And what happens when T1a and T1b cannot be distinguished?
approvals.why: NCCN routes it to resection on low-quality evidence. The propensity-matched cohort used to argue for surveillance found equivalent overall survival but recurrence-free survival differences of 66.1% against 86.7% (P=0.052) and, in adenocarcinoma only, 61.4% against 82.6% (P=0.066) on 55 matched patients — two near misses in the same direction. That cohort never reports T stage, so it cannot inform the T1a-versus-T1b split on which nodal risk turns; nodal status is unknown in its papillectomy arm by definition; and the immortal time the surgical arm had to survive is unaddressed. Without a standing position this will be decided by whoever is in the room.
approvals.audit: Specimen findings including T substage and which margins were assessed, decision taken, recurrence, and nodal status at any later resection.

approvals.q: Is adjuvant chemotherapy offered to all resected stage II and III patients, or preferentially by histologic subtype?
approvals.why: ESPAC-3's primary analysis was negative (hazard ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.66–1.11, P=0.25), it was never powered for its ampullary subgroup, and no hypothesis test for ampullary-only survival is reported anywhere in the paper. The two subtype-stratified cohorts do not carry equal weight: the positive one allocated adjuvant therapy at tumour board by stage, nodes and CA 19-9 with no adjustment of any kind and reports a whole-cohort result running the other way (hazard ratio 1.124, P=0.608), while the negative one propensity-matched on those same selection drivers and handled immortal time bias — though its intervals do not exclude a 25% to 35% relative risk reduction. A third cohort found benefit confined to the intestinal subtype. NCCN's algorithm is staged while its regimen lists are subtyped.
approvals.audit: Registry: subtype as reported, adjuvant regimen, completion, recurrence site, overall survival.

approvals.q: Is a subtype call with interobserver κ 0.39 accepted as a basis for choosing the adjuvant regimen?
approvals.why: Not an evidence question but a governance one. The guidelines organise their regimen lists around the subtype; the reproducibility data say five blinded observers agree in 23% of cases, 40% of tumours are mixed, pure intestinal morphology is present in only 6%, the survival difference appears only after the mixed cases are force-assigned, and even then the subtype fails multivariable analysis at P=0.39. PERIPAN's own conclusion is that the prognostic and predictive role of subtype remains unclear. The group should decide whether the regimen follows the subtype or the stage.
approvals.audit: Proportion of resections subtyped on the invasive component; proportion mixed or tubular-NOS; whether the subtype changed the recommendation.

approvals.q: Is mismatch-repair testing a reflex on every ampullary carcinoma, or ordered by indication?
approvals.why: PERIPAN recommends reflex testing on every case regardless of subtype, graded low evidence, on an assertion that the deficiency rate is comparable to colorectal cancer; the 2021 ESGE ampullary guideline recommended against routine molecular and immunohistochemical testing of ampullary biopsies, and NCCN recommends somatic profiling only for metastatic patients who are candidates for therapy. The published prevalence runs from 4.3% (1 of 23 early-onset cases) to 15% (18 of 119 tested cases), so one in six is the upper end of a range rather than an established figure. The result is both a treatment test and a germline trigger, which is the argument for reflex testing independent of the prevalence estimate. [PAYER]
approvals.audit: Testing completion rate on resected carcinoma, the local deficiency rate measured rather than assumed, and germline referrals generated.

approvals.q: What minimum number of examined lymph nodes does this programme hold itself to at pancreatoduodenectomy for ampullary cancer?
approvals.why: A National Cancer Database analysis of 8,127 resections places the inflection point at 20, but it is cited here from its abstract only and the derivation of the threshold could not be checked; PERIPAN defers to the pancreatic minimum, where proposals run from 11 to 17; the largest pathology series had a median of 11 with only 48% of specimens reaching 12. That series also showed the N0 and N1 survival curves converging once 12 or more nodes were examined, which is an argument that adequate sampling changes the meaning of the N category rather than only its precision. A number that is not written down is not audited.
approvals.audit: Nodes examined per specimen against the stated minimum, and the proportion of short counts triggering re-examination of the specimen.

approvals.q: Who owns post-papillectomy surveillance, and when does it stop?
approvals.why: ESGE says at least 5 years and sets no endpoint, and its 3-, 6- and 12-month schedule has no stated derivation. Recurrence after a histological R0 was still 13% at 5 years in 798 patients, which is the honest reason to continue. The ten-year argument rests on one patient recurring at 9.75 years in a cohort whose mean follow-up was shorter than its own mean time to recurrence. There are no stopping-rule data and no competing-risk analysis in this population.
approvals.audit: Named owner; interval adherence at 3, 6 and 12 months and annually; recurrences detected after year 5.

approvals.q: In polyposis, does the programme adopt the ESGE and BSG ampullary-appearance intervals alongside the Spigelman stage, and which guideline column does it follow for the Spigelman intervals themselves?
approvals.why: ACG, ASGE, BSG and ESGE differ at every Spigelman stage, most sharply at stages III and IV, and only ESGE and BSG set an interval on the ampulla. About 50% of duodenal cancers in these patients are periampullary and the Spigelman stage does not predict them. Both halves are weak: the score has never been formally validated and two of its four components require histology that the same guidelines discourage obtaining, while the ampullary intervals of 5, 3 and 1 year appear in the guideline text as proposed intervals that seem safe, with no citation and no modelling. [EXPERTISE]
approvals.audit: Ampullary appearance documented at each surveillance endoscopy; interval set against interval achieved; non-attendance.

approvals.q: Who owns the NCCN, ESGE and PERIPAN update checks, on what cycle, and who resolves the ESPAC-3 discrepancy in the extracted NCCN text before this page goes live?
approvals.why: This page was built from a machine-converted guideline extraction that carries no version string and that misstates ESPAC-3 on one page while stating it correctly on another. The full-text read of ESPAC-3 confirms the discrepancy from the trial side: there is no significant ampullary disease-free or overall survival result in that trial to report, because the subgroup was never tested. No version of this page should be published without that reconciled against the published guideline.
approvals.audit: Named owner, guideline edition and date recorded, agreed update cycle, and a signed-off note on the ESPAC-3 wording.

approvals.q: Does the programme count argon plasma coagulation or radiofrequency ablation at the index papillectomy as part of an R0 resection, or as evidence of residual disease?
approvals.why: The largest European series reports both answers: R0 for adenoma after papillectomy was 80.2%, and 65.9% once the 14.4% of cases that had index-session ablation are counted as probable R2 resections. Which convention the programme adopts determines its own reported R0 rate, its surveillance intensity for those patients, and whether its figures can be compared with anyone else's.
approvals.audit: Ablation at the index session recorded separately from R status for every papillectomy, with recurrence by both conventions.

approvals.q: What does the programme do with an indeterminate (Rx) resection margin after papillectomy?
approvals.why: An Rx margin accounted for 206 of 798 specimens (25.8%) in the Japanese national cohort, carried a hazard ratio of 2.38 for recurrence against R0, and by 5 years had the same cumulative recurrence as a frankly positive margin (34% each). It is the commonest ambiguous result in this pathway and ESGE offers no recommendation for it. Treating it as positive for surveillance purposes is this page's convention, not evidence.
approvals.audit: Proportion of papillectomy specimens reported Rx, the stated local cause for each, and recurrence by R0, R1 and Rx.

approvals.q: Which definition of recurrence does the programme's papillectomy dashboard use — counting residual disease found at the first surveillance endoscopy, or only events after a documented negative examination?
approvals.why: The two large cohorts in the literature differ on exactly this, which is why their recurrence rates (18.3% and 16.1%) are not comparable, and the choice determines whether the programme's own figure measures initial resection quality or genuine recurrence. One cohort's internal data show the consequence: more recurrence after en bloc than piecemeal resection, because piecemeal patients had their residual disease reclassified.
approvals.audit: Recurrence reported both ways, with time to event, out to at least 5 years and not truncated at 2.

approvals.q: Does the programme use the ESPAC-4 and PRODIGE-24 regimens in ampullary cancer at all, and if so what is said at consent?
approvals.why: Both trials excluded nonductal tumours by protocol and neither reports a single ampullary patient. PRODIGE-24 produced grade 3 or 4 toxicity in 75.9% of a population restricted to performance status 0–1 and age under 80, with no disease-free survival benefit in those aged 70 or over; ESPAC-4 gained 2.5 months of median survival, reported early, with the benefit confined to R0 patients. Ampullary carcinoma has roughly double the resected median survival of pancreatic cancer and no randomised evidence that any adjuvant chemotherapy helps. Offering these regimens is a defensible choice about risk tolerance; it should be made once, in writing, rather than case by case.
approvals.audit: Regimen given, subtype and stage, documented statement of the evidence source at consent, toxicity, completion and recurrence.

approvals.q: Does the programme measure its own preoperative biopsy false-negative rate for invasive carcinoma, and at what rate does it change the gate 1 threshold?
approvals.why: The published range is 20% to 40% and every supporting figure is shifted by selection — the 8.9% major-discrepancy rate was computed on the 36% of patients who had follow-up pathology, and the 32% occult-carcinoma rate came after 44.3% of papillectomies had been excluded for a malignant biopsy or suspicious appearance. A local rate is the only one that can be acted on, and the roughly one-in-three wrong-indication rate in the European series suggests that most programmes do not know theirs.
approvals.audit: Final histology against preoperative biopsy for every resected ampullary lesion, by number and site of biopsies, reported annually.

Pages used: clinical presentation, workup and treatment algorithms for ampullary adenoma and adenocarcinoma; postoperative adjuvant treatment and surveillance; Principles of Stent Management; Principles of Surgical Technique; Pathologic Analysis including Histologic Subtyping; Principles of Systemic Therapy (neoadjuvant, adjuvant, metastatic); Principles of Radiation Therapy; AJCC tables; and the Discussion. Known defect: the Principles of Systemic Therapy adjuvant page states that ESPAC-3 demonstrated significant improvements in disease-free and overall survival with adjuvant gemcitabine or fluorouracil versus observation in resectable ampullary adenocarcinoma, and quotes median survivals of 23.0 and 23.6 months for fluorouracil-leucovorin and gemcitabine — neither claim matches the published periampullary trial (PMID 22782416), and those medians correspond to the ESPAC-3 pancreatic cohort. The guideline's own Discussion states the position correctly. Confirm against the published PDF before quoting. The full-text read of ESPAC-3 on 7 October 2026 confirms the discrepancy from the trial side: the published periampullary trial reports no significant disease-free or overall survival result for ampullary adenocarcinoma, adjusted or otherwise, because the ampullary subgroup was never powered and no hypothesis test for it was performed.
nccnpanc: National Comprehensive Cancer Network. Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma. NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology. Programme-supplied machine-converted extraction, consulted 6 October 2026; no version string in the extraction. Used for the operative and specimen questions ampullary disease shares with pancreatic cancer: the 1 mm margin convention and its acknowledged extrapolation from rectal cancer data, the SMA (retroperitoneal, uncinate) margin and specimen inking, the randomised and meta-analytic evidence against extended lymphadenectomy, and the minimum-lymph-node-yield proposals of 11 to 17.
ajcc8: Amin MB, Edge SB, Greene FL, et al., editors. AJCC Cancer Staging Manual. 8th edition. Springer International Publishing, 2017. Ampulla of Vater T, N, M definitions, prognostic groups and histologic grade, as reproduced with permission in the NCCN ampullary adenocarcinoma guideline (Tables 1 to 3).
cap: College of American Pathologists. Cancer Protocol Template for carcinoma of the Ampulla of Vater. The source of the 1 mm positive-margin definition and of the minimum data set that NCCN abbreviates; PERIPAN recommends either the CAP protocol or its own expanded PERIPAN pathology report template.
who5: WHO Classification of Tumours Editorial Board. Digestive System Tumours. WHO Classification of Tumours, 5th edition. IARC, 2019. The classification that PERIPAN refines and extends — PERIPAN adds medullary, micropapillary, gastric-type, rhabdoid and osteoclastic carcinomas as entities to report separately from tubular adenocarcinomas of intestinal, pancreatobiliary, mixed and NOS subtype. Consulted indirectly through PERIPAN rather than read directly for this draft.
periwork: PERIPAN Consensus Guidelines, full document with all 38 consensus questions, 51 recommendations, evidence grading, comments and proposed actions, plus the PERIPAN pathology report template, published as supporting information to United European Gastroenterol J. 2025;13(7):1048-1068. The summary tables were used for this draft; the full supplement should be read before the page is ratified. Two process items promised in the PERIPAN methods are not reported anywhere in the published paper and should be looked for in the supplement: the independent Jury Committee's AGREE II quality score across 23 items and six domains, and the audience agreement percentages from the public vote at the Brescia meeting. Note also that 33 of 57 draft recommendations reached 80% agreement in the first Delphi round and the remainder were revised and re-voted until they passed, so the final figure of 50 of 51 measures iteration rather than first-pass agreement.

provenance: This is a second draft, revised on 7 October 2026 after a full-text read of the paper depot behind it. There is still no ratified Memorial Hermann roadmap for ampullary tumours, no alignment worksheet behind it, and no institutional position has been taken on any of the fifteen items in the approvals list — the page is a proposal for a multidisciplinary group to argue with, not a statement of practice. What the full-text read changed. Twenty-eight of the thirty-five cited papers were read in full and abstracted with their authors' stated limitations and an independent critique, and the revision moved the page in three material ways. First, ESPAC-3 can no longer be cited as establishing adjuvant benefit in ampullary cancer: the trial was never powered for its ampullary subgroup, reports no hypothesis test for ampullary-only survival anywhere, and the ampullary medians of 40.6, 57.8 and 70.8 months appear without a P value; its primary analysis was negative (hazard ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.66–1.11, P=0.25), its adjusted analysis (0.75, 0.57–0.98, P=0.03) adjusted for four variables on two of which the observation arm was prognostically worse at baseline, and in its 96 intrapancreatic bile duct patients chemotherapy was numerically worse than observation. Adjuvant chemotherapy remains on the page and is now graded C and offered as a reasonable choice rather than a demonstrated benefit. Second, the subtype question has been rewritten as an asymmetric dispute rather than a tie: the reproducibility study is the ceiling on all of it (κ 0.39, all five observers agreeing in 23% of 232 cases, 40% of tumours mixed, pure intestinal only 6%, survival differing only after the mixed cases were force-assigned, and the subtype failing multivariable analysis at P=0.39), and of the two adjuvant cohorts the positive one allocated treatment at tumour board by prognosis with no adjustment of any kind and reports a whole-cohort result running the other way (hazard ratio 1.124, P=0.608) while the negative one propensity-matched on the actual selection drivers and handled immortal time bias — so the divergence is explained by cohort and method rather than by chance, although the negative result is still underpowered to exclude a modest benefit. Third, the European comparison of papillectomy with surgical ampullectomy is now read for its indication finding first: final histology was neither adenoma nor adenocarcinoma in 24.2% of papillectomies and 14.8% of surgical ampullectomies while advanced disease was found in 10.9% and 36.6%, so roughly a third of the procedures in both arms were done for the wrong indication; papillectomy R0 for adenoma falls from 80.2% to 65.9% once index-session ablation is counted as a probable R2 resection; and papillectomy failed in roughly two-thirds of T1 cancers. Borrowed evidence. ESPAC-4 and PRODIGE-24 are trials of resected pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma that excluded nonductal tumours by design and report no ampullary patients; the page now says so wherever it uses them, as it does for the preoperative biliary drainage trial (cancer of the pancreatic head, plastic stents, no ampullary subgroup), BILCAP (biliary tract), ABC-02 (advanced biliary tract, ampullary patients included but not counted), X-ACT (colon) and the randomised evidence against extended lymphadenectomy (pancreatic). Cited from abstract only. Five papers were sought and not obtained, and every string that uses them says so: the National Cancer Database node-yield analysis (PMID 38353072), the intraductal ultrasound and transpapillary biopsy series (22319960), the 91-patient malignancy prediction cohort (23442830), the EUS preoperative evaluation series (30834717) and the 14-patient ampullary neuroendocrine tumour series (27457864). BILCAP (30922733) and ABC-02 (20375404) were also not part of the full-text read and are quoted from their abstracts and from guideline text. Guideline sources, unchanged from the first draft. The programme-supplied machine-converted extraction of the NCCN Ampullary Adenocarcinoma guideline, which carries no version string and which misstates ESPAC-3 on its adjuvant systemic-therapy page while stating it correctly in its discussion (see nonpm, and approvals item 10) — the full-text read confirms that discrepancy from the trial side; the NCCN Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma extraction for the margin, specimen and lymphadenectomy questions the two diseases share; the Brescia PERIPAN international multidisciplinary consensus guidelines of 29 July 2025 for the anatomic definitions, the subtype definitions, the biopsy and specimen-handling recommendations and the reflex mismatch-repair position; the ESGE guideline on endoscopic management of ampullary tumours of 2021 and the ESGE polyposis guideline of 2019 for the endoscopic and familial gates; and AJCC 8th edition staging as reproduced in NCCN. Every PMID in refs was verified against PubMed on 6 October 2026 to confirm it resolves to the paper cited. Readers should know that nine of eleven main ESGE ampullary recommendations are strong on low-quality evidence, that almost every PERIPAN recommendation is low evidence or expert opinion with its promised AGREE II quality score and audience vote never reported, and that PERIPAN's 30% threshold for the mixed subtype has no stated derivation. Where the sources disagree — on whether subtype should direct adjuvant therapy, on surveillance intervals by Spigelman stage, on whether mismatch-repair and molecular testing is reflex, indication-driven or discouraged, on the minimum node yield, and on what to do with an invasive carcinoma found in a margin-negative papillectomy specimen — the page shows the disagreement and places the choice in a flagnote and in approvals rather than resolving it. Evidence strings carry both halves of every result. Grades fell in eleven places on this revision and rose nowhere, and each downgrade is explained in the note on the string it belongs to; no recommendation was removed, because the roadmap's positions stand and the page's job is to say how well supported they are. Grades are deliberately low across the benign end of the pathway: most of what is done there rests on retrospective series and expert consensus, and grade D is used where that is the truth. This page does not replace clinician judgement, and every numeric criterion must be verified against the current source before use.
